topics.name: Learning Roadmap: 17 Phases

beginner.content:
How to use this roadmap

• The phases below take you from the first variable to production-grade full-stack JavaScript. Each phase is a module in this course, with worked examples and interview questions.
• Essential phases are needed by every JavaScript developer. Important phases make you effective. Optional and Advanced phases depend on your stack.
• Follow the order: later phases assume the earlier ones (closures before async, async before fetch, fetch before React data loading).
PhaseTopicsPriority
1Fundamentals, variables, data types, operatorsEssential
2Conditions, loops, functionsEssential
3Arrays, strings, objectsEssential
4Scope, hoisting, closures, thisEssential
5Modern JavaScript and destructuringEssential
6Array methods, Map, SetEssential
7DOM manipulation and eventsEssential for browser development
8Promises, async/await, event loopEssential
9Fetch API and REST integrationEssential
10Classes, prototypes, OOPImportant
11Modules, error handling, debuggingEssential
12Browser APIs and web storageImportant
13Security and testingEssential for production
14TypeScriptEssential for your chosen stack
15ReactEssential for your chosen stack
16Node.js and ExpressOptional with Spring Boot
17Advanced internals and performanceAdvanced

intermediate.content:
A realistic study plan

• Phases 1-3: about 2-3 weeks. Write small programs daily; do not just read.
• Phases 4-6: about 2 weeks. This is where most beginners get stuck, so redo the closure and this examples until you can predict the output.
• Phases 7-9: about 3 weeks. Build a small app that loads data from an API and renders it in the DOM.
• Phases 10-13: about 3 weeks. Turn that app into modules, add error handling and tests.
• Phases 14-17: choose by your stack. With Spring Boot as the back end, TypeScript and React matter more than Node.js and Express.

expert.content:
Checkpoints that show you are ready to move on

• After phase 3: you can solve array/string problems without looking up syntax.
• After phase 6: you can explain, without notes, why for (var i...) with setTimeout prints the same number.
• After phase 9: you can build a page that fetches, validates, renders and handles failure of a REST call.
• After phase 13: you can explain XSS and CSRF and write a unit test with a mocked dependency.

interviewQA: In what order should JavaScript be learned?

Language core first (types, control flow, functions), then scope/closures/this, then modern syntax and collections, then the DOM, then asynchronous code and fetch, then OOP, modules and tooling, and only then frameworks and Node. Each layer depends on the previous one.
Which phases are optional if the back end is Spring Boot?
Node.js and Express. You still need fetch, TypeScript and a front-end framework, because Spring Boot serves JSON and the browser needs JavaScript to consume it.

beginner.content:
What is JavaScript?

• JavaScript is a lightweight, interpreted (JIT-compiled) programming language that runs in every web browser and, via Node.js, on the server too.
• It is dynamically typed - variable types are determined at runtime, not declared upfront.
• JavaScript is single-threaded but achieves concurrency through an event loop and asynchronous callbacks, promises, and async/await.
• Three ways to declare variables: var (function-scoped, legacy), let (block-scoped, reassignable), const (block-scoped, cannot be reassigned).

Fresher Notes

  • JavaScript is the programming language of the web. It runs in the browser (and on servers with Node.js) and makes pages interactive.
  • You can try it in the browser console, in a <script> tag or in a .js file.
  • Basics: variables (let, const), functions, objects and arrays.

Worked Example 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The JavaScript engine (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) parses source into an AST, compiles it (interpreter plus optimizing JIT compiler) and runs it on a call stack. Asynchronous work (timers, network, UI events) is handled by the host environment, which queues callbacks. The event loop repeatedly takes the next task when the stack is empty, and drains the microtask queue (promises) after each task.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to run JS: inline script, external file, type="module", the browser console, Node.js (node file.js), and bundlers/dev servers (Vite). Script loading: defer (after parsing, in order), async (as soon as loaded), module scripts (deferred by default).
codeExamples:
<script type="module" src="/main.js"></script>
<script defer src="/analytics.js"></script>
// main.js
import { greet } from "./greet.js";
document.querySelector("h1").textContent = greet("Abaji");

// OUTPUT:
// the heading shows the greeting after the document is parsed

intermediate.content:
var vs let vs const - Scoping Differences

var is function-scoped and hoisted (accessible before declaration, as undefined). let/const are block-scoped and live in the "temporal dead zone" until their declaration line runs - accessing them earlier throws a ReferenceError.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • JavaScript is dynamically typed, single-threaded and event-driven: long work must be asynchronous so the page stays responsive.
  • Use const by default, let when reassigning, and avoid var.
  • Use strict equality ===; == performs type coercion and causes surprises.

Senior Notes

  • The runtime has a call stack, a heap, a task queue and a microtask queue; the event loop moves callbacks onto the stack.
  • Modern JS is delivered as ES modules, transpiled and bundled for older browsers (Babel, Vite, esbuild).
  • Use TypeScript for larger codebases to catch type errors early.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Common beginner mistakes: using == instead of ===, forgetting that var leaks out of blocks, blocking the main thread with long loops, mutating shared objects, ignoring errors from promises, and not using strict mode or modules. Modules are strict by default.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance basics: do not block the main thread (split long work, use workers), minimize DOM writes, debounce frequent events, load code lazily (dynamic import) and measure with the Performance panel.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a small progressive enhancement. The page works without JavaScript, and a script adds a live character counter to a textarea with minimal code.

beginner.content:
Functions in JavaScript

Functions are first-class citizens in JavaScript - they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. Three common syntaxes:
1. Function Declaration
2. Function Expression
3. Arrow Function (ES6, shorter syntax, does NOT have its own this)

Fresher Notes

  • A function is reusable code: function add(a, b) { return a + b; } or an arrow function const add = (a, b) => a + b.
  • Scope decides where a variable is visible: global, function and block scope.
  • Functions are values: you can store them in variables, pass them as arguments and return them.

Worked Example 1

Memoize.

Worked Example 2

Debounce.

Practice Exercise 1

Defaults, rest and spread.

Practice Exercise 2

Higher-order function.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A function call creates an execution context with its own scope (variable environment) linked to the outer scope (lexical environment). Name lookups walk this scope chain. Arguments are passed by value (references are copied for objects). Arrow functions do not create their own this or arguments; they capture them from the surrounding scope.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: declarations, expressions, arrow functions, immediately invoked functions (IIFE), generators (function*), async functions, methods and constructors. Parameters: defaults, rest, destructuring. Call styles: call, apply, bind.

intermediate.content:
Closures

A closure is a function that "remembers" the variables from the scope it was created in, even after that outer scope has finished executing. Closures are the mechanism behind private state and factory functions in JavaScript.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Default parameters (function f(x = 1)), rest parameters (...args) and spread calls (f(...list)).
  • Function declarations are hoisted; function expressions and arrow functions are not usable before definition.
  • Arrow functions have no own this or arguments.

Senior Notes

  • Higher-order functions (map, filter, reduce, custom) enable composition and callbacks.
  • Pure functions (no side effects) are easier to test and reason about.
  • Currying, memoization and debouncing are common function patterns in real applications.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on hoisting, forgetting to return, mutating parameters, arrow functions as object methods (wrong this), callbacks that lose this, and unbounded recursion (stack overflow). Use pure functions and explicit returns.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: avoid creating functions inside hot loops when not needed, memoize pure expensive functions, debounce or throttle event handlers, and prefer iteration to deep recursion (no guaranteed tail-call optimization).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a throttle for scroll handlers and a retry helper for flaky network calls, both small higher-order functions reused across the app.

beginner.content:
Primitive vs Reference Types

JavaScript has 7 primitive types - string, number, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, bigint - and one reference type, object (arrays and functions are objects too). Primitives are copied by value; objects are copied by reference.

typeof null famously returns "object" - a long-standing JavaScript bug kept for backward compatibility, not a design choice.
codeExamples:
console.log(typeof "hello");   // "string"
console.log(typeof 42);        // "number"
console.log(typeof true);      // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined); // "undefined"
console.log(typeof null);      // "object" - the famous bug
console.log(typeof Symbol());  // "symbol"
console.log(typeof {});        // "object"
console.log(typeof []);        // "object" - arrays are objects too

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Primitive types: number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint. Everything else is an object.
  • Primitives are copied by value; objects and arrays are copied by reference.
  • Use typeof to check a type (remember typeof null is "object").

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

BigInt.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Primitives are immutable values stored directly; objects are heap-allocated and accessed by reference. Operators coerce types by well-defined rules (ToPrimitive, ToNumber, ToString). Numbers are IEEE-754 doubles, so integers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1. strings are UTF-16 sequences.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Conversion tools: Number(), parseInt/parseFloat, String(), Boolean(), unary plus, JSON.stringify/parse, Intl formatters, Date and Temporal (new), Symbol, BigInt, typed arrays.

intermediate.content:
== vs === and Truthy/Falsy Coercion

== coerces operands to the same type before comparing (often surprising); === compares both value and type with no coercion, and is almost always the right default. Falsy values are: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN - everything else (including "0" and []) is truthy.
codeExamples:
console.log('5' + 3);   // "53" - + with a string triggers concatenation
console.log('5' - 3);   // 2   - - only makes sense numerically, so '5' is coerced to a number

console.log(0 == '0');    // true  - '0' coerced to 0
console.log(0 === '0');   // false - different types, no coercion
console.log([] == false); // true  - [] coerces to "" then to 0

if ([]) console.log('arrays are truthy, even empty ones'); // this runs

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Type coercion converts values automatically: "5" * 2 is 10, "5" + 2 is "52".
  • Falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN; everything else is truthy.
  • Number precision: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3; use integers (cents) or toFixed/Intl for money.

Senior Notes

  • Use Number.isInteger, Number.isNaN and explicit conversion (Number(x)) instead of relying on coercion.
  • BigInt handles integers beyond 2^53; do not mix it with numbers.
  • Compare objects by identity; use deep-equality helpers or structuredClone for copies.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: comparing with == across types, NaN checks with ===, dates in local time (off-by-one days), JSON with undefined or functions silently dropped, and mixing BigInt and Number (TypeError). Be explicit about conversions and time zones.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: strings are immutable (use arrays and join for many concatenations in hot code), typed arrays are fast for numeric data, avoid unnecessary conversions in loops, and use Map/Set for lookups instead of arrays.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: money and dates. Store amounts as integer minor units, format with Intl, and send dates as ISO-8601 UTC strings.

beginner.content:
Common Array Methods

• push()/pop() - add/remove from the end.
• unshift()/shift() - add/remove from the start.
• splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) - remove/insert anywhere, mutates the array.
• slice(start, end) - returns a shallow copy of a portion, does NOT mutate.
codeExamples:
let fruits = ['apple', 'banana'];
fruits.push('cherry');           // ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
fruits.pop();                    // ['apple', 'banana']
fruits.unshift('mango');         // ['mango', 'apple', 'banana']
fruits.splice(1, 1, 'kiwi');     // removes 'apple', inserts 'kiwi' -> ['mango', 'kiwi', 'banana']
console.log(fruits.slice(0, 2)); // ['mango', 'kiwi'] - fruits itself unchanged by slice

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • An array is an ordered list: const items = [1, 2, 3]. Access by index, length gives the size.
  • Add and remove: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice.
  • Transform with map, filter with filter, summarize with reduce, search with find/includes.

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Arrays are objects with numeric keys and a length property, optimized by engines into contiguous storage when elements are of the same kind. Methods like push and pop are O(1); shift, unshift and splice move elements and cost O(n). Higher-order methods call your callback once per element and return new arrays (map, filter) or a single result (reduce).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Families: mutators (push, pop, splice, sort, reverse, fill), accessors (slice, concat, join, indexOf, includes, at), iterators (forEach, map, filter, reduce, some, every, find, findIndex, flatMap), and modern non-mutating versions (toSorted, toSpliced, toReversed, with).

intermediate.content:
map(), filter(), reduce() - The Functional Trio

map() transforms every element into a new array (same length). filter() keeps only elements matching a condition (shorter or equal length). reduce() folds the array down into a single value. forEach() is similar to map() but always returns undefined - it's for side effects, not building a new array.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • map/filter/reduce/forEach/some/every/find/sort/flat/flatMap are the everyday tools.
  • sort mutates and sorts as strings by default; pass a comparator (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
  • Non-mutating alternatives: toSorted, toReversed, with, spread copies.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer immutable updates (spread, map, filter) especially in React state.
  • Chaining creates intermediate arrays; for very large data use a single reduce or loops.
  • Array.from, Set and Map help dedupe and index data efficiently.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: sort without a comparator, mutating arrays used in React state, forEach with async callbacks, reduce without an initial value on empty arrays (TypeError), and using indexOf for objects. Use immutable patterns and for...of with await.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: chained map/filter create temporary arrays; for very large inputs use one pass (reduce or a loop) or generators. Searching arrays is O(n): use Set/Map for repeated lookups.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a table view. Filter by search text, sort by a chosen column, paginate, and compute totals without mutating the source data.

beginner.content:
Working with Objects

Properties can be accessed with dot notation (obj.key) or bracket notation (obj["key"]) - bracket notation is required when the key is dynamic or not a valid identifier. Object.keys(), Object.values(), and Object.entries() extract an object's keys, values, or [key, value] pairs as arrays.

Fresher Notes

  • An object stores key-value pairs: const user = { name: "Abaji", age: 30 }. Access with user.name or user["name"].
  • Methods are functions stored as properties.
  • Useful helpers: Object.keys, Object.values, Object.entries, Object.assign.

Worked Example 1

Shallow copy trap.

Worked Example 2

Map for counting.

Practice Exercise 1

Spread merge and safe access.

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Objects are dynamic collections of properties; each property has a key (string or symbol), a value and attributes (writable, enumerable, configurable). Property lookup walks the prototype chain until found. Spread and Object.assign copy own enumerable properties shallowly; getters and setters are accessor properties.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: Object.keys/values/entries/fromEntries, Object.freeze/seal, defineProperty, structuredClone, destructuring with renaming and defaults, computed keys, Symbol keys, Proxy and Reflect, WeakMap for private data.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Shorthand properties, computed keys { [key]: value }, spread { ...a, ...b } for merging.
  • Optional chaining user?.address?.city and nullish coalescing value ?? "default" handle missing data.
  • Object.freeze makes an object shallow-immutable; Object.defineProperty controls property behaviour.

Senior Notes

  • Objects are mutable references; copy before changing shared data. Use structuredClone for deep copies.
  • Prefer Map when keys are not strings or order and size matter; prefer plain objects for records.
  • Prototype chain: objects inherit from their prototype; class is syntax over prototypes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: shallow copies of nested data, iterating with for...in (includes inherited keys), using objects as maps with user-controlled keys (prototype pollution via __proto__), and comparing objects with ===. Use Map for dynamic keys, structuredClone for copies and Object.hasOwn.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: objects with stable shapes (same keys in the same order) are fastest; adding and deleting properties dynamically deoptimizes them. Use Map for frequently changing key sets and avoid delete in hot paths.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: normalizing API data. Convert a list into an id-indexed Map for O(1) lookups and derive related views without duplicating objects.

beginner.content:
for...of vs for...in

for...of iterates over the VALUES of an iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets). for...in iterates over the enumerable KEYS/property names of an object (and, for arrays, over the indices as strings) - using for...in on an array is almost always a mistake.

Fresher Notes

  • Conditionals: if/else, switch and the ternary cond ? a : b.
  • Loops: for, while, do...while, for...of (values) and for...in (keys).
  • break leaves a loop and continue skips to the next iteration.

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

switch with grouped cases.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Control flow in JavaScript is evaluated by the engine statement by statement. Conditions are converted to booleans by truthiness rules; switch compares with strict equality; loops re-evaluate their condition each iteration. for...of calls the iterator protocol (Symbol.iterator), which is why it works with arrays, strings, Maps, Sets and generators.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: if/else if, ternary, switch, optional chaining and nullish coalescing as conditional operators, for, while, do...while, for...of, for...in, for await...of, labeled break/continue, and array iteration methods.

intermediate.content:
switch and the Ternary Operator

switch compares with strict equality and falls through to the next case unless you break. The ternary operator condition ? a : b is a compact if/else expression that produces a value.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Use for...of for arrays and iterables, Object.entries for objects, and avoid for...in on arrays.
  • Truthiness drives conditions; be explicit when 0 or "" are valid values.
  • Short-circuit: a && b, a || b, a ?? b.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer array methods (map/filter/reduce) for transformations and loops for control flow or performance-critical code.
  • Guard clauses (early returns) reduce nesting and improve readability.
  • Avoid mutating the collection you iterate over.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: off-by-one in for loops, modifying an array while iterating, assignment (=) instead of comparison in conditions, missing break in switch (fall-through), for...in on arrays, async work in forEach, and infinite loops. Use for...of, guard clauses and explicit comparisons.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Loop performance rarely matters until data is large. Prefer algorithmic improvements (Set lookups, early exit with some/find or break, single pass) over micro-optimizations; avoid nested loops over big lists (O(n²)).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: process work in batches with a loop and concurrency limit, so the page or server stays responsive and external APIs are not overloaded.

topics.name: Closures Deep Dive - The Loop + setTimeout Trap

beginner.content:
The Classic var-in-a-loop Closure Bug

This site's "Functions & Scope" topic already introduces closures via a counter-factory example. The single most common closure interview question builds on that idea: what happens when a closure is created inside a loop using var?

Because var is function-scoped (not block-scoped), every callback created inside the loop shares the SAME single i variable - by the time the callbacks actually run, the loop has already finished and i holds its final value.

Fresher Notes

  • A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.
  • Classic use: a counter or private state: the inner function keeps access to the outer variable.
  • The famous trap: var in a loop with setTimeout prints the same value, because all callbacks share one variable.

Worked Example 1

IIFE fix for var.

Worked Example 2

Stale closure in a timer.

Practice Exercise 1

The loop trap and fixes.

Practice Exercise 2

Private state with a closure.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Each function object stores a hidden [[Environment]] reference to the scope where it was created. When it runs, its new scope links to that environment, so variable lookups can reach outer variables, even if the outer function has returned. The engine keeps the captured environment alive for as long as the closure is reachable.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Closures appear as: factories (makeCounter), module pattern (IIFE with private state), callbacks that capture context, currying and partial application, memoization caches, event handlers, and React hooks (state kept in closures per render). let in loops creates a fresh binding per iteration.

intermediate.content:
The Fix: let (or an IIFE)

let is block-scoped, so each loop iteration gets its OWN fresh binding of i - each closure captures a different variable instead of sharing one.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • let creates a new binding per loop iteration, which fixes the loop trap; with var use an IIFE or a function that captures the value.
  • Closures power callbacks, event handlers, memoization, module patterns and React hooks.
  • Each call of the outer function creates a separate closure with its own variables.

Senior Notes

  • Closures keep their captured variables alive; accidentally capturing large objects can cause memory leaks.
  • Stale closures (a callback seeing old values) are a common React bug; use dependency arrays or functional updates.
  • Understand lexical scoping: the scope chain is fixed where the function is written, not where it is called.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

The loop trap, stale closures and leaks. A closure captures variables, not values, so later changes are visible; but a value copied into a parameter is frozen. In React, an effect that uses state without listing it as a dependency sees an old value. Captured large objects stay in memory while the closure lives.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Closures are cheap, but each creates a function object and keeps its environment alive. Creating thousands of closures per render or per item is fine; capturing huge arrays or DOM nodes in long-lived listeners causes leaks. Remove listeners and clear timers when done.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a once-only function, a rate limiter and a simple event emitter, all implemented with closures and no classes.

beginner.content:
The Document Object Model (DOM)

The DOM is a tree-structured, in-memory representation of an HTML page. JavaScript can read and modify this tree - adding, removing, or changing elements - and the browser re-renders the page to match.

Fresher Notes

  • The DOM is the browser model of the page. JavaScript selects elements and changes them.
  • Select with document.querySelector / querySelectorAll or getElementById.
  • Change content with textContent, attributes with setAttribute, classes with classList, styles with style.

Worked Example 1

Worked Example 2

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The browser parses HTML into the DOM tree (nodes), CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, performs layout (geometry) and paint (pixels). Changing the DOM can trigger style recalculation, layout and repaint. Reading layout values (offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect) after writes forces the browser to compute layout immediately (forced reflow).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

APIs: selection (querySelector(All), closest, matches), creation (createElement, template, cloneNode), insertion (append, before, insertAdjacentHTML), attributes and dataset, classList, events and delegation, IntersectionObserver, MutationObserver, requestAnimationFrame.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Create and insert nodes: createElement, append, prepend, remove.
  • Prefer textContent over innerHTML for user text to avoid XSS.
  • Batch DOM updates (document fragments or build then insert once) to avoid repeated layout work.

Senior Notes

  • Reading layout properties (offsetHeight) after writes forces layout; group reads and writes.
  • Event delegation: one listener on a parent handles events from many children.
  • Frameworks (React, Angular) manage the DOM for you with virtual DOM or fine-grained updates; know the raw API for debugging.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: innerHTML with user input (XSS), adding listeners to every row (use delegation), reading and writing layout in alternating loops (layout thrashing), querying the DOM repeatedly inside loops, and forgetting to remove listeners from removed nodes. Cache references, batch changes and sanitize input.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Rendering performance: animate transform and opacity (compositor-friendly), use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates, virtualize long lists, and keep the DOM small. Measure with the browser Performance panel.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an accessible filterable list without a framework. Typing filters rows, the live region announces the count, and event delegation handles row selection.

beginner.content:
Handling Events

addEventListener() attaches a callback that runs when a specific event (click, input, submit, etc.) fires on an element. Multiple listeners can be attached to the same event without overwriting each other (unlike the old onclick = ... style).

Fresher Notes

  • Events are things that happen in the page: clicks, key presses, form submits, loads. You react with element.addEventListener("click", handler).
  • The handler receives an event object with details (target, key, clientX).
  • Remove listeners with removeEventListener using the same function reference.

Worked Example 1

Cancel many listeners at once.

Worked Example 2

Custom event.

Practice Exercise 1

Delegated click handling.

Practice Exercise 2

Form submit with validation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

When an event fires, the browser builds the propagation path from the window down to the target, runs capture listeners along the way, then the target listeners, then bubble listeners back up. Listeners run synchronously, one after another, on the main thread, so a slow listener blocks rendering and other events.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: capture, once, passive, signal. Event types: mouse, keyboard, pointer, touch, input, change, submit, focus, scroll, resize, drag and drop, custom events, observers (IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver). Delegation uses closest and matches.

intermediate.content:
Event Bubbling & Delegation

Events "bubble" upward from the target element through its ancestors. Event delegation exploits this: attach ONE listener to a parent element instead of one listener per child - useful for dynamically added elements.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Event flow: capture (down), target, bubble (up). Most listeners run in the bubble phase.
  • preventDefault() stops the default action (form submit, link follow); stopPropagation() stops bubbling.
  • Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent and uses event.target / closest.

Senior Notes

  • Passive listeners ({ passive: true }) improve scroll performance; { once: true } auto-removes a listener.
  • Custom events (new CustomEvent) decouple components.
  • Debounce or throttle high-frequency events (scroll, resize, input).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: anonymous functions that cannot be removed, forgetting that this/event.target differ (currentTarget vs target), handlers that block, stopPropagation overuse (breaks other code), and listeners on removed elements. Keep references, use delegation and AbortController.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

High-frequency events (scroll, mousemove, resize, input) can fire dozens of times per frame. Debounce or throttle, use requestAnimationFrame, passive listeners and observers instead of polling.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: keyboard shortcuts and accessibility. One document-level listener maps key combinations to commands and ignores typing inside inputs.

beginner.content:
Destructuring & the Spread/Rest Operators

Destructuring unpacks values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables in one line. The spread operator (...) expands an iterable; the rest operator collects remaining items.

Fresher Notes

  • Destructuring unpacks values: const [a, b] = arr and const { name, age } = user.
  • Arrow functions are a short function syntax: (a, b) => a + b.
  • Spread ... expands arrays and objects; rest ... collects the remaining items.

Worked Example 1

Swap and rest.

Worked Example 2

Arrow function this.

Practice Exercise 1

Parameters, defaults and renaming.

Practice Exercise 2

Immutable update with spread.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Destructuring is syntax for pulling values out using the iterator protocol (arrays) or property access (objects), with defaults applied when the value is undefined. Spread uses the same protocols in the other direction. Arrow functions are compiled to function objects whose this, arguments and super are lexical.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: nested destructuring, computed property keys in patterns, function parameter destructuring with defaults, destructuring in loops (for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(o))), swapping, returning multiple values, and spread for copying and merging arrays and objects.

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Defaults and renaming: const { name: userName = "guest" } = obj.
  • Destructure in parameters: function f({ id, qty = 1 }) {}.
  • Swap variables: [a, b] = [b, a].

Senior Notes

  • Spread creates shallow copies; nested objects are still shared.
  • Use object spread for immutable updates: { ...state, count: state.count + 1 }.
  • Arrow functions capture this lexically and cannot be constructors.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: destructuring null or undefined (TypeError), forgetting that defaults apply only for undefined (not null), shallow copies assumed deep, parentheses needed for object destructuring assignment, and overly deep patterns that hurt readability. Provide a default object and keep patterns simple.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Spread and destructuring allocate new arrays and objects; in tight loops or with very large arrays this adds up (spreading a million elements into a call can exceed the argument limit). Use loops, push or concat for large data.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: reducers and state updates stay readable with destructuring and spread, always returning new objects so UI frameworks can detect changes.

beginner.content:
Asynchronous JavaScript

A Promise represents a value that will be available later (pending → fulfilled or rejected). async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises that lets asynchronous code read like synchronous code.

Fresher Notes

  • JavaScript is single threaded, so slow operations (network, timers) are asynchronous. A Promise represents a value that will arrive later.
  • async functions return promises and await pauses until a promise settles.
  • Handle errors with try/catch around await or .catch() on promises.

Worked Example 1

Timeout with AbortController.

Worked Example 2

Promise.race for a timeout.

Practice Exercise 1

Sequential vs parallel.

Practice Exercise 2

Error handling.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An async function runs synchronously until the first await; at an await it returns a promise to the caller and registers the rest of the function as a continuation in the microtask queue when the awaited promise settles. Promise reaction jobs are microtasks, so they run before the next timer or I/O callback. Errors become rejections of the returned promise.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: Promise.all/allSettled/race/any, Promise.withResolvers, async iterators with for await, AbortController, timers, queueMicrotask, streams, worker threads and message passing. Patterns: retry with backoff, concurrency pools, timeouts, caching promises.

intermediate.content:
Promise.all() - Running Async Operations in Parallel

Awaiting Promises one-by-one runs them sequentially. Promise.all() runs independent async operations concurrently and resolves once ALL of them finish (or rejects as soon as any one fails).

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Promise states: pending, fulfilled, rejected. .then, .catch and .finally chain callbacks.
  • Promise.all runs promises in parallel and fails fast; allSettled waits for all; race takes the first; any the first success.
  • Do not make independent calls sequentially with await in a loop when they could run in parallel.

Senior Notes

  • Unhandled rejections crash Node processes and log errors in browsers; always handle them.
  • Cancel work with AbortController; add timeouts to network calls.
  • Concurrency limits (batches or a pool) protect servers and APIs from overload.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting await (a promise object used as a value), unhandled rejections, await in forEach, sequential awaits for independent work, swallowing errors in catch, creating promises in a loop without limits, and mixing callbacks and promises. Use Promise.all with map and always handle rejections.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Throughput comes from parallelism with bounds. Fire independent requests together, cap concurrency to protect servers, cache in-flight promises to deduplicate identical requests, and use AbortController to cancel obsolete work.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a search box. Debounce typing, cancel the previous request when a new one starts, ignore stale responses and show loading and error states.

beginner.content:
this - Determined by HOW a Function is Called

Unlike variable scope, this is NOT determined by where a function is defined - it is determined by how the function is called at the call site.
• Regular function call: this is the global object (undefined in strict mode/modules).
• Method call (obj.method()): this is the object before the dot.
• Arrow functions: do NOT have their own this - they lexically inherit this from the enclosing scope where they were defined.

Fresher Notes

  • this refers to the object that calls the function. In a method call obj.method(), this is obj.
  • In a plain function call, this is undefined (strict mode) or the global object.
  • Arrow functions do not have their own this; they use the this of the surrounding code.

Worked Example 1

this in callbacks.

Worked Example 2

new and this.

Practice Exercise 1

Practice Exercise 2

Arrow function field in a class.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

this is determined at call time (except in arrow functions). Binding rules in order: new (new object), explicit (call/apply/bind), implicit (the object before the dot), default (undefined in strict mode, global otherwise). Arrow functions resolve this lexically like any other variable from the enclosing scope.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls: bind (partial application too), arrow functions, self = this (old style), class fields with arrows, Function.prototype.call/apply, globalThis, Reflect.apply, queueMicrotask with bound callbacks, and passing context arguments (arr.map(fn, thisArg)).

intermediate.content:
The Classic "this Lost in a Callback" Bug

A regular function passed as a callback loses its intended this because it gets called as a plain function invocation, not as obj.method(). Arrow functions fix this by inheriting this from where they're defined.

call(), apply(), and bind() - Explicit this Control

These let you explicitly set what this should be for a function call, overriding the normal call-site rules.
• call(thisArg, ...args) - invokes immediately, arguments passed individually.
• apply(thisArg, argsArray) - invokes immediately, arguments passed as an array.
• bind(thisArg) - returns a NEW function permanently bound to thisArg, does not invoke immediately.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How is 'this' determined in JavaScript?By how a function is called (the call site) - not where it's defined, except for arrow functions
Why don't arrow functions have their own 'this'?They lexically inherit 'this' from the enclosing scope at the time they're defined - useful for preserving 'this' inside callbacks
Difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?call/apply invoke immediately (args individually vs as an array); bind returns a new permanently-bound function without invoking it

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • call, apply and bind set this explicitly.
  • Extracting a method loses its this: const f = obj.method; f().
  • In event handlers with regular functions, this is the element; with arrow functions it is the outer this.

Senior Notes

  • In classes, bind methods or use arrow function fields when passing them as callbacks.
  • Prefer closures or arrow functions over bind in modern code; be explicit about context.
  • In modules and classes the code runs in strict mode, so a lost this becomes undefined and fails fast.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: passing methods as callbacks (lost this), arrow functions as object methods (this is outer), using this inside nested regular functions, and assuming this in event handlers. Use arrow callbacks, bind, or class arrow fields.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Bound functions and per-instance arrow fields create one function per instance, which costs memory in large collections; prototype methods are shared. Choose per-instance arrows only where the method is passed around as a callback.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: React class components needed bound handlers; modern code uses function components and closures, where this is not involved at all, which removes this class of bugs.

beginner.content:
try / catch / finally

Wrap risky code in try; if it throws, execution jumps to catch instead of crashing the program. finally always runs, whether or not an error occurred - useful for cleanup.

Fresher Notes

  • Use try { ... } catch (e) { ... } finally { ... } to handle runtime errors without crashing.
  • Throw errors with throw new Error("message").
  • Errors have name, message and stack.

Worked Example 1

Error cause chain.

Worked Example 2

Cleanup in finally.

Practice Exercise 1

Custom error and handling.

Practice Exercise 2

Global error reporting.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

When an exception is thrown the engine unwinds the call stack looking for a catch. If none exists, it becomes an uncaught error (browser: window error event; Node: process crash for unhandled rejections). Errors capture a stack trace when created. try/finally guarantees cleanup code runs in all exit paths including return.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: built-in errors (TypeError, RangeError, SyntaxError), custom subclasses with codes, cause chaining, AggregateError (Promise.any), Promise.allSettled, error boundaries (React), global handlers, Error.captureStackTrace (V8), and Result-style returns for expected failures.

intermediate.content:
Error Handling in async/await Code

With Promises, errors are handled via .catch(). With async/await, a rejected Promise throws inside the async function, so plain try/catch works around await calls.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does finally always run?Yes - whether the try block succeeds, throws and is caught, or even if catch itself throws
How do you handle errors in async/await code?Wrap the await calls in a regular try/catch block - a rejected Promise throws inside the async function
Can you throw something other than an Error object?Yes, JS allows throwing any value, but throwing Error objects is best practice since they carry a stack trace and message

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Custom errors: class ValidationError extends Error with extra fields.
  • Async errors: promises reject; use try/catch with await or .catch.
  • finally always runs, which is useful for cleanup.

Senior Notes

  • Do not swallow errors silently; log with context and rethrow or return a meaningful result.
  • Validate input early and fail with clear messages; use error codes for programmatic handling.
  • In browsers use window.onerror and unhandledrejection for global reporting; in Node handle unhandledRejection.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: empty catch blocks, catching and logging without rethrowing when the caller must know, throwing strings, losing the cause, using exceptions for normal control flow, and not handling promise rejections. Throw Error objects, add context and rethrow.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Throwing and catching is slower than normal returns and stack capture costs time. Use exceptions for exceptional cases, not for loops or validation of expected input; return result objects for those. Keep catch blocks narrow.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an API client that converts HTTP failures into typed errors, retries transient ones, and a UI that shows a friendly message while logging full details.

beginner.content:
Class Syntax

ES6 class syntax is syntactic sugar over JavaScript's existing prototype-based inheritance - under the hood, it's still prototypes. Classes give a cleaner, more familiar syntax for defining constructors and methods.

Fresher Notes

  • A class is a template for objects: class User { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } greet() { ... } }. Create with new User("Abaji").
  • Inheritance uses extends and super.
  • Classes are syntax over JavaScript prototypes.

Worked Example 1

Composition.

Worked Example 2

Prototype view.

Practice Exercise 1

Class with private state.

Practice Exercise 2

Inheritance.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A class declaration creates a constructor function and puts methods on its prototype. Instances link to the prototype through [[Prototype]], so a method lookup walks the chain. extends sets up the prototype chain between constructor and prototype objects; super calls the parent. Private fields (#x) are stored in hidden per-instance slots and are inaccessible outside the class body.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Features: constructors, instance and static fields and methods, getters/setters, private fields and methods, static blocks, inheritance and super, instanceof, Symbol.iterator on classes, mixins, and new.target. Class expressions and the Object.create/prototype style are alternatives.

intermediate.content:
Inheritance with extends and super

extends creates a subclass; super(...) calls the parent constructor and must be called before using this in the subclass constructor. Overriding a method and still calling the parent's version uses super.methodName().

Static Methods

static methods belong to the class itself, not to instances - called as ClassName.method(), useful for utility/factory functions related to the class.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Are JS classes truly a new inheritance model?No - they are syntactic sugar over the existing prototype chain; typeof still reports functions, and prototype-based mechanics still apply underneath
Why must super() be called before using 'this' in a subclass constructor?The parent constructor is responsible for setting up the base object; JS enforces this ordering so 'this' is never used before the object is properly initialized
What are static methods used for?Utility or factory functions that belong to the class itself rather than to any particular instance

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Static members belong to the class (static create()); private fields use #name; getters and setters control access.
  • Class fields can be declared directly: count = 0;.
  • Methods are on the prototype, shared by all instances; arrow function fields are per-instance.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer composition over deep inheritance; use small classes or plain functions where state is not needed.
  • Private fields (#) are truly private; underscore names are only a convention.
  • Be careful with this when passing methods as callbacks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting super() before using this in a subclass constructor (ReferenceError), calling a class without new (TypeError), deep hierarchies, mutable static state, and exposing internals instead of using private fields. Prefer composition and small classes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Instances created from classes are optimized well by engines when their shape is stable: initialize all fields in the constructor in the same order. Large numbers of per-instance arrow functions increase memory; use prototype methods.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a small domain model with validation in the constructor, immutable value objects (frozen) and a repository class that hides storage.

beginner.content:
Named Exports vs Default Export

ES6 modules let you split code across files. A module can have multiple named exports and at most ONE default export. This example is illustrative multi-file code (it cannot run as a single snippet) showing how the pieces connect.

Fresher Notes

  • Modules split code into files. export exposes functions or values and import brings them into another file.
  • Use <script type="module"> in the browser; Node supports ES modules with .mjs or "type": "module".
  • Each module has its own scope, so nothing leaks to the global object.

Worked Example 1

Re-exports (barrel file).

Worked Example 2

Module scope.
codeExamples:
<script type="module">
  const secret = 1;            // not on window
  console.log(typeof window.secret, import.meta.url.endsWith(".html"));
</script>

// OUTPUT:
// undefined true

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Named and default exports.

Practice Exercise 2

Lazy loading.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

ES modules are statically analysable: imports and exports are declared at the top level, so the engine can build the dependency graph before running any code. Each module is loaded once, evaluated in dependency order, and exports are live bindings (importers see updates to exported variables). Module code is always strict mode.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: named exports, default export, re-exports (export * from), namespace imports (import * as m), side-effect imports, dynamic import(), import.meta, import maps in browsers, top-level await, JSON and CSS module imports (with import attributes). CommonJS (require) is the older Node system.

intermediate.content:
Why Modules Matter

• Avoid polluting the global namespace - each module has its own scope.
• Explicit dependencies - you can see exactly what a file imports and exports.
• Enables tree-shaking - bundlers can drop unused exports from the final bundle.
• import statements are hoisted and modules are only evaluated once, even if imported from multiple files (cached).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How many default exports can a module have?At most one - but it can have any number of named exports alongside it
Do named imports need to match the exported name?Yes, unless aliased with 'as' during import (e.g. import { add as sum })
Is a module re-evaluated every time it's imported?No - modules are evaluated once and cached; subsequent imports reuse the same module instance

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • Named exports (export const x, import { x }) and one default export (export default).
  • Dynamic import (await import("./x.js")) loads code on demand.
  • Modules are singletons: they run once and the exports are shared.

Senior Notes

  • Bundlers (Vite, esbuild, webpack) combine and optimize modules; tree shaking removes unused exports.
  • Avoid circular imports; they cause partially initialized bindings.
  • Prefer named exports for better refactoring and tooling support.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: circular dependencies, mixing CommonJS and ESM incorrectly, forgetting file extensions in browser imports, barrel files that defeat tree shaking and slow tests, and default exports that make renames inconsistent. Prefer named exports and direct imports.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: split bundles by route with dynamic import, rely on tree shaking (side-effect free modules and static imports), preload critical modules (modulepreload) and cache with content hashes.
codeExamples:
<link rel="modulepreload" href="/assets/app.3f9a1c.js">
const routes = { "/reports": () => import("./reports.js"), "/admin": () => import("./admin.js") };
const page = await routes[location.pathname]?.();

// OUTPUT:
// initial bundle 120 kB; reports chunk 48 kB loaded on demand

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a plugin system loading modules by name at runtime, with a small contract each plugin exports.

beginner.content:
fetch() - Making HTTP Requests

fetch(url) returns a Promise that resolves with a Response object once the HTTP response headers arrive (the body isn't parsed yet). Call .json() on the response to parse the body as JSON - that also returns a Promise.

Fresher Notes

  • fetch(url) makes HTTP requests and returns a promise of a Response. Read the body with await res.json().
  • Check res.ok (status 200-299); fetch does not reject on HTTP error codes, only on network failure.
  • Send data with options: method, headers and body.

Worked Example 1

Parallel requests.

Worked Example 2

Upload a file.

Practice Exercise 1

GET and POST with checks.

Practice Exercise 2

Timeout.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

fetch returns a promise that resolves once response headers arrive; the body is a stream read by json(), text(), blob() or arrayBuffer() (each can be consumed once). The browser enforces CORS, applies HTTP caching, cookies (per credentials mode) and follows redirects. Network failures reject with TypeError; HTTP errors resolve with ok = false.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: method, headers, body (string, FormData, Blob, URLSearchParams, stream), mode, credentials, cache, redirect, signal, keepalive. Helpers: Request, Response, Headers, URL, URLSearchParams, streaming with res.body.getReader().

intermediate.content:
The fetch() Gotcha: It Doesn't Reject on HTTP Errors

fetch()'s Promise only rejects on a network failure (e.g. no connection, DNS error) - a 404 or 500 response is still a "successful" fetch as far as the Promise is concerned. You must manually check response.ok or response.status.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
When does fetch()'s Promise reject?Only on network-level failures (no connection, DNS failure, CORS block) - NOT on HTTP error status codes like 404 or 500
How do you detect an HTTP error status with fetch()?Manually check response.ok (true for 2xx status) or response.status after the fetch resolves
Why does .json() return a Promise too?Reading and parsing the response body is itself an asynchronous streaming operation

expert.content:
Mid-Level Notes

  • POST JSON: fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(data) }).
  • Query strings: use URLSearchParams to encode safely.
  • Cancel with AbortController; credentials and CORS are controlled by credentials and mode.

Senior Notes

  • CORS is enforced by the browser; the server must send the right headers; preflight requests precede non-simple requests.
  • Retry only idempotent requests, with backoff; show loading and error states in the UI.
  • Avoid putting secrets in front-end code; keep tokens in httpOnly cookies where possible.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: assuming fetch rejects on 4xx/5xx, forgetting Content-Type on JSON posts, reading the body twice, setting Content-Type for FormData uploads (breaks the boundary), ignoring CORS errors, and no timeouts or retries. Wrap fetch in a helper that handles these.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: reuse connections (HTTP/2), cache GETs with proper headers or an in-memory cache, deduplicate in-flight requests, use compression, request only needed fields and use pagination. Prefetch data before navigation when possible.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an API client module used by the whole app, handling base URL, auth header, JSON, errors, timeouts and one retry for network failures.

subTopics.name: Phase 1 · Fundamentals, Variables, Data Types, Operators (Essential)

topics.name: Variables: var, let and const

beginner.content:
Declaring variables

• A variable is a named container for a value. JavaScript has three keywords: var (old, function-scoped), let (block-scoped, reassignable) and const (block-scoped, cannot be reassigned).
• Use const by default, let when the value must change, and avoid var in new code.
• const prevents re-assignment, not mutation: a const object or array can still have its contents changed.
• Names are case-sensitive, may contain letters, digits, _ and $, and cannot start with a digit. Use camelCase for variables and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for true constants.

intermediate.content:
Scope and redeclaration differences

• var ignores block boundaries (if, for) and can be redeclared; let and const cannot be redeclared in the same scope.
• A let/const variable exists from the start of its block but cannot be touched before its declaration line: that gap is the temporal dead zone.
• A top-level var in a classic script becomes a property of window; let/const do not.

expert.content:
Freezing, and what "constant" really means

• Object.freeze makes an object shallowly immutable. Nested objects stay mutable unless they are frozen too.
• In strict mode, writing to a frozen object throws; in sloppy mode it silently does nothing, which hides bugs. Always use "use strict" or ES modules (which are strict by default).
• Prefer const plus immutable updates ({...obj, x: 1}) over mutating shared objects.

interviewQA: Difference between var, let and const?

var is function-scoped, hoisted with value undefined and re-declarable. let and const are block-scoped, live in the temporal dead zone until declared, and cannot be re-declared. const additionally forbids re-assignment (not mutation).
Can you change a const array?
Yes. const protects the binding, not the value: push, pop and index assignment all work. Re-assigning the variable (arr = []) throws a TypeError.
What is the temporal dead zone?
The span from the start of a block until a let/const declaration is executed. Reading the variable there throws a ReferenceError, unlike var which would give undefined.

topics.name: Data Types and Type Conversion

beginner.content:
The eight types

• Primitives (immutable, compared by value): string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol.
• Object (compared by reference): plain objects, arrays, functions, dates, maps and so on.
• typeof reports the type as a string. Two famous quirks: typeof null is "object" (a historical bug) and typeof a function is "function".
• undefined means "no value assigned"; null means "intentionally empty".
codeExamples:
console.log(typeof "hi");        // string
console.log(typeof 42);          // number
console.log(typeof 10n);         // bigint
console.log(typeof true);        // boolean
console.log(typeof undefined);   // undefined
console.log(typeof null);        // object  (quirk)
console.log(typeof Symbol("id"));// symbol
console.log(typeof [1, 2]);      // object
console.log(Array.isArray([1])); // true  (the reliable array check)
console.log(typeof function () {}); // function

intermediate.content:
Number precision and conversion

• Numbers are 64-bit floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Compare with a tolerance or work in integer cents.
• Explicit conversion: Number("42"), parseInt("42px", 10), String(42), Boolean("").
• Implicit coercion happens with + (string concatenation wins if either side is a string) and with ==. Other arithmetic operators convert to numbers.
• Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including "0", [] and {}.
codeExamples:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);                 // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON); // true
console.log("5" + 3);                   // "53"  (concatenation)
console.log("5" - 3);                   // 2     (numeric)
console.log(Number("12px"));            // NaN
console.log(parseInt("12px", 10));      // 12
console.log(Boolean("0"), Boolean([])); // true true
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER);   // 9007199254740991

expert.content:
Equality and Object.is

• === compares without coercion and is what you should use. == applies a long list of coercion rules (null == undefined is true, "1" == 1 is true, [] == false is true).
• NaN is the only value not equal to itself; use Number.isNaN(x), not the global isNaN which coerces first.
• Object.is treats NaN as equal to itself and distinguishes +0 from -0.
• Objects are compared by reference: two separate {} are never equal.
codeExamples:
console.log(null == undefined, null === undefined); // true false
console.log("1" == 1, "1" === 1);                    // true false
console.log(NaN === NaN, Number.isNaN(NaN));         // false true
console.log(isNaN("abc"), Number.isNaN("abc"));      // true false
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN), Object.is(0, -0));  // true false
console.log({} === {});                              // false

const a = { id: 1 };
const b = a;
console.log(a === b);                                // true (same reference)

interviewQA: Why is typeof null "object"?
An early implementation tagged values by type bits, and null (the null pointer, all zero bits) matched the object tag. It was never fixed for backwards compatibility. Check null with value === null.
What is the difference between null and undefined?

undefined is the default for a missing value (unassigned variable, missing property, no return). null is an explicit "no value" assigned by the programmer. null == undefined is true, null === undefined is false.
Numbers are binary IEEE-754 doubles and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation. Use a tolerance (Number.EPSILON) or integer minor units such as paise or cents.

topics.name: Operators

beginner.content:
Everyday operators

• Arithmetic: + - * / % ** (% is remainder, ** is exponent).
• Assignment: = += -= *= /= %= **=, plus the logical forms &&= ||= ??=.
• Comparison: === !== < > <= >=. Logical: && (and), || (or), ! (not).
• Increment and decrement: i++ returns the old value, ++i returns the new one.

intermediate.content:
Short-circuit, nullish coalescing and optional chaining

• a || b returns the first truthy operand; a && b returns the first falsy one. Both return an operand, not a boolean.
• a ?? b falls back only when a is null or undefined, so 0, "" and false are kept. Prefer it over || for defaults.
• obj?.a?.b stops and returns undefined if any link is nullish, instead of throwing.
• ??= assigns only when the target is nullish.
codeExamples:
const settings = { volume: 0, theme: "" , user: null };

console.log(settings.volume || 50);  // 50   (0 is falsy: probably a bug)
console.log(settings.volume ?? 50);  // 0    (0 is a real value)
console.log(settings.theme  ?? "dark"); // "" (kept)

console.log(settings.user?.profile?.city);   // undefined, no TypeError
console.log(settings.save?.());              // undefined, method missing

settings.language ??= "en";
console.log(settings.language);              // en

expert.content:
Precedence, spread of operands and bitwise tricks

• Precedence (high to low, simplified): () then !/unary then ** then * / % then + - then comparisons then === then && then ||/?? then ternary then assignment. When unsure, add parentheses.
• ?? cannot be mixed with || or && without parentheses (a SyntaxError), which prevents ambiguity.
• Bitwise operators work on 32-bit integers: x | 0 truncates, x & 1 tests odd, 1 << n is 2^n. Use them for flags, not as a replacement for Math.floor on large numbers.
codeExamples:
console.log(2 + 3 * 4 ** 2);      // 50
console.log((2 + 3) * 4);         // 20
console.log(true || false && false); // true  (&& binds tighter)

const READ = 1, WRITE = 2, EXEC = 4;
let perm = READ | WRITE;          // 3
console.log((perm & WRITE) !== 0); // true  (has WRITE)
perm &= ~WRITE;                    // remove WRITE
console.log(perm);                 // 1
console.log(7.9 | 0, -7.9 | 0);    // 7 -7  (truncation toward zero)

interviewQA: Difference between || and ??
|| falls back for any falsy left side (0, "", false, NaN, null, undefined). ?? falls back only for null or undefined, so legitimate falsy values are preserved.
What does optional chaining return when a link is missing?
undefined, and the rest of the chain is skipped (short-circuited). It never creates the missing property.
Difference between i++ and ++i?
Postfix i++ evaluates to the old value then increments; prefix ++i increments then evaluates to the new value. They differ only when the expression result is used.

topics.name: Conditions: if, switch and the Ternary

beginner.content:
Making decisions

• if / else if / else runs the first branch whose condition is truthy.
• The ternary cond ? a : b is an expression; use it for simple value choices, not for side effects.
• switch compares with ===. Each case must end with break (or return) or execution falls through into the next case.

intermediate.content:
Guard clauses and lookup tables

• Deeply nested if blocks are hard to read. Handle the invalid cases first and return early (guard clauses).
• A long switch or else if chain that only maps a key to a value is better as an object or Map lookup.
• switch(true) works for ranges but is usually clearer as an if chain.

expert.content:
Truthiness traps and switch fall-through

• if (arr.length) is the idiom for "not empty", but if (arr) is true even for [].
• if (value) rejects 0 and "" which may be valid input. Test explicitly: value !== undefined && value !== null.
• A switch without break keeps running the next case body even if its test fails. Lint rules (no-fallthrough) catch this.

interviewQA: What happens if you omit break in a switch case?
Execution falls through into the next case body regardless of its label, until a break, return or the end of the switch. It is occasionally used on purpose for grouped cases.
Does switch use == or ===?
Strict equality (===). switch("1") does not match case 1.
When is a lookup object better than switch?
When the branches only map a key to a value. It is shorter, data-driven and easy to extend; a switch is better when each branch runs different logic.

topics.name: Loops: for, while, for...of and for...in

beginner.content:
Repeating work

• for (init; test; update) is the classic counted loop; while tests before each pass; do...while runs at least once.
• for...of iterates the values of any iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets).
• for...in iterates the enumerable keys of an object. Do not use it on arrays.
• break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next pass.

intermediate.content:
Choosing the right loop

• Need the index too? for (const [i, v] of arr.entries()).
• Iterate an object's own data with Object.entries(obj) and for...of, which avoids inherited keys that for...in would include.
• forEach cannot be stopped with break and does not wait for await in its callback. Use for...of when you need either.
• Labels (outer:) let break/continue target an outer loop.

expert.content:
Loop pitfalls

• Infinite loops: a missing update or a condition that never becomes false. Always make sure the loop variable moves toward the exit.
• Closures in loops: let creates a fresh binding per iteration; var shares one binding (see the closure phase).
• Modifying while iterating: removing items from an array inside for...of skips elements. Iterate a copy or build a new array with filter.
• Sparse arrays: for...in and forEach skip holes, for...of visits them as undefined.

interviewQA: Difference between for...of and for...in?
for...of iterates the values of an iterable. for...in iterates enumerable string keys of an object, including inherited ones, so it is meant for plain objects, not arrays.
Can you break out of forEach?
No. break/continue are not allowed in the callback and return only ends that one call. Use for...of, some() or every() instead.
Why does a for loop with var and setTimeout print the same number?
var has one function-scoped binding shared by all callbacks. By the time the timers fire the loop has finished and the variable holds its final value. let creates a new binding per iteration.

topics.name: Functions: Parameters, Return Values and Callbacks

beginner.content:
Writing functions

• A function groups reusable logic. It receives parameters, and the caller passes arguments. Without a return it returns undefined.
• Default parameters fill in missing arguments: function greet(name = "guest").
• Rest parameters collect extra arguments into a real array: function sum(...nums).
• Functions are values: store them in variables, pass them as arguments (callbacks) and return them.

intermediate.content:
Pure functions, side effects and IIFEs

• A pure function returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself. Pure functions are easy to test and reason about.
• A side effect is anything observable besides the return value: mutating an argument, writing to a variable outside, logging, network calls. Keep them at the edges of the program.
• Arguments that are objects are passed by sharing the reference: mutating the parameter mutates the caller's object.
• An IIFE (immediately invoked function expression) runs once and creates a private scope.

expert.content:
Function internals worth knowing

• Every function has a name and a length (the number of parameters before the first default or rest parameter).
• The old arguments object is array-like and absent from arrow functions. Prefer rest parameters.
• Parameter defaults are evaluated at call time, in their own scope, and can reference earlier parameters.
• Currying and partial application build specialised functions from general ones; composition chains small functions into pipelines.
• Recursion needs a base case; very deep recursion throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. Convert to a loop when depth is unbounded.

interviewQA: Difference between parameters and arguments?
Parameters are the names in the function definition. Arguments are the actual values supplied when calling it.
What is a pure function and why prefer it?
It always returns the same result for the same inputs and has no side effects. That makes it predictable, cacheable and trivial to unit test.
Are objects passed by value or by reference?
JavaScript always passes by value, but the value of an object variable is a reference. So mutating the object through the parameter is visible to the caller, while re-assigning the parameter is not.

topics.name: Arrays: Creating, Reading and Changing

beginner.content:
Array basics

• An array is an ordered, zero-indexed list that can hold any mix of values. length is always one more than the highest index.
• Add/remove at the end: push/pop. At the start: unshift/shift (slower, they re-index).
• slice(start, end) copies a section without changing the original. splice(start, count, ...items) removes/inserts in place.
• Modern accessors: at(-1) reads from the end; includes tests membership; indexOf finds a position.
codeExamples:
const langs = ["Java", "JS"];
langs.push("Python");          // ["Java", "JS", "Python"]
langs.unshift("C");            // ["C", "Java", "JS", "Python"]
console.log(langs.at(-1));     // Python
console.log(langs.indexOf("JS"), langs.includes("Go")); // 2 false

const part = langs.slice(1, 3);       // ["Java", "JS"]  original untouched
langs.splice(1, 1, "Kotlin", "Go");   // replaces "Java" with two items
console.log(langs);   // ["C", "Kotlin", "Go", "JS", "Python"]

intermediate.content:
Copying, sorting and the mutation trap

• Assignment copies the reference: const b = a makes both names point at one array. Use [...a] or a.slice() for a shallow copy and structuredClone(a) for a deep copy.
• sort() mutates and compares as strings by default. Always pass a comparator for numbers.
• Newer non-mutating twins: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with (ES2023).
• Build arrays with Array.from({length: 3}, (_, i) => i); avoid new Array(3), which creates holes.

expert.content:
Shallow vs deep copy, and flat structures

• Spread and slice copy only the first level. Nested arrays/objects are still shared between the copies.
• structuredClone deep-copies plain data, Dates, Maps and Sets but throws on functions. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) drops undefined, functions and Dates (turns them into strings).
• flat(depth) and flatMap flatten nested arrays; destructuring swaps values without a temp variable.
• Arrays are objects: extra properties and holes are possible, and typeof [] is "object".

interviewQA: Why does [10, 9, 1].sort() give [1, 10, 9]?
Without a comparator sort converts items to strings and orders them by UTF-16 code units, so "10" comes before "9". Pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
How do you copy an array?
Shallow: [...arr] or arr.slice(). Deep: structuredClone(arr). A plain assignment only copies the reference.
Difference between slice and splice?
slice returns a copy of a range and leaves the original alone. splice removes/inserts elements in the original array and returns the removed items.

topics.name: Strings: Methods, Searching and Formatting

beginner.content:
Working with text

• Strings are immutable: every method returns a new string.
• Common methods: length, toUpperCase, toLowerCase, trim, slice, includes, startsWith, endsWith, indexOf, replace/replaceAll, split, padStart, repeat.
• Template literals use backticks, allow ${expression} interpolation and multi-line text.
codeExamples:
const s = "  JavaScript Rocks  ";
console.log(s.trim().toUpperCase());        // JAVASCRIPT ROCKS
console.log(s.trim().slice(0, 4));          // Java
console.log("a-b-c".split("-"));            // ["a", "b", "c"]
console.log("2".padStart(3, "0"));          // 002
console.log("ha".repeat(3));                // hahaha
console.log("x.y.z".replaceAll(".", "/"));  // x/y/z

const name = "Asha", n = 3;
console.log(`${name} has ${n * 2} items`); // Asha has 6 items

intermediate.content:
Regular expressions and comparison

• replace with a string only changes the first match; use a regex with the g flag or replaceAll.
• match, matchAll, test and named groups extract structured text.
• Compare strings with localeCompare for human-correct ordering (accents, case) and Intl for locale-aware formatting.
• Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji) are two UTF-16 units, so "😀".length is 2. Use [...str] or Array.from to count code points.
codeExamples:
console.log("a.b.c".replace(".", "-"));      // a-b.c  (first only)
console.log("a.b.c".replace(/\./g, "-"));    // a-b-c

const m = "Order #4821 on 2026-10-19".match(/#(?<id>\d+) on (?<date>[\d-]+)/);
console.log(m.groups.id, m.groups.date);     // 4821 2026-10-19

console.log(["b", "a", "C"].sort());                       // ["C", "a", "b"]
console.log(["b", "a", "C"].sort((x, y) => x.localeCompare(y))); // ["a", "b", "C"]
console.log("😀".length, [..."😀"].length);  // 2 1
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN").format(1234567.5)); // 12,34,567.5

expert.content:
Security and performance with strings

• Never build HTML, SQL or URLs by concatenating user text. Escape or use safe APIs (textContent, encodeURIComponent, parameterised queries).
• Repeated += in a loop is fine in modern engines (ropes), but joining an array with join is clearer for building large output.
• Tagged templates call a function with the string parts and values, enabling safe escaping, i18n and styled-component libraries.

interviewQA: Are strings mutable in JavaScript?
No. Strings are immutable primitives; methods like toUpperCase return a new string and index assignment (s[0] = "x") silently does nothing.
How do you replace all occurrences of a substring?
Use replaceAll("a", "b") or replace with a global regex such as /a/g. replace with a plain string changes only the first match.
What is a template literal?
A backtick-delimited string that supports ${expression} interpolation, multi-line text and tagged-template functions.

topics.name: Objects: Properties, Copying and Descriptors

beginner.content:
Object basics

• An object is a collection of key-value pairs. Keys are strings or symbols; values can be anything, including functions (methods).
• Read with dot (obj.name) or bracket (obj["first name"], or a computed key) notation. Delete with delete obj.key.
• Shorthand: { name, age } and shorthand methods { greet() {} }. Test a key with "key" in obj or Object.hasOwn(obj, "key").
• Object.keys, Object.values, Object.entries and Object.fromEntries convert between objects and arrays.

intermediate.content:
Merging, immutable updates and iteration order

• Spread {...a, ...b} and Object.assign({}, a, b) make shallow copies; later keys win.
• Update immutably: {...user, age: 26} instead of mutating, which is the pattern React state relies on.
• Property order: integer-like keys ascending first, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols.
• Use a Map instead of an object when keys are not strings, when you add and remove keys often, or when you need reliable size and order.

expert.content:
Property descriptors and defensive objects

• Each property has a descriptor: value, writable, enumerable, configurable (or get/set). Object.defineProperty sets them.
• Object.freeze (no add/remove/change), Object.seal (no add/remove, values changeable), Object.preventExtensions (no add).
• Getters and setters compute or validate on access. A Proxy can intercept reads, writes and deletes for validation, logging or reactivity.
• Object.create(null) makes a prototype-less dictionary, immune to keys like __proto__ and toString.

interviewQA: How do you check whether an object has a property?
"key" in obj checks own and inherited keys. Object.hasOwn(obj, "key") (or obj.hasOwnProperty) checks only own keys. obj.key !== undefined fails when the value is genuinely undefined.
Difference between Object.freeze and const?
const stops re-assigning the variable. Object.freeze stops adding, removing and changing the properties of the object itself (shallowly).
When should you use a Map instead of an object?
When keys are not strings/symbols, when entries are added and removed frequently, when insertion order and size matter, or to avoid prototype key collisions.

topics.name: Scope Chain and Hoisting

beginner.content:
Where a variable is visible

• Global scope: visible everywhere. Function scope: visible inside the function. Block scope (let/const): visible inside the { } block.
• When a name is used, JavaScript looks in the current scope, then the enclosing scope, and so on outward to global: the scope chain. Inner scopes can read outer variables, never the reverse.
• An inner variable with the same name shadows the outer one.

intermediate.content:
Hoisting

• Before running, the engine registers declarations of the scope ("hoisting"). Function declarations are hoisted completely, so they can be called before the line that defines them.
• var is hoisted and initialised to undefined. let/const/class are hoisted but uninitialised (temporal dead zone).
• Function expressions (including arrows) assigned to a variable follow the variable's rule, not the function rule.

expert.content:
Lexical scope and the execution context

• JavaScript uses lexical (static) scope: a function's scope is decided by where it is written, not where it is called.
• Each call creates an execution context with a variable environment and a reference to its outer environment; that link is the scope chain.
• Function declarations inside blocks behave differently in strict mode and sloppy mode. Avoid them; use const fn = () => {} in blocks.
• The name of a class or let in a block is private to that block, which makes blocks a lightweight way to avoid polluting the outer scope.

interviewQA: What is hoisting?

The engine processes declarations before executing code. var variables become available as undefined, function declarations are available with their body, and let/const/class exist but throw if accessed before their declaration (temporal dead zone).
What is lexical scope?
Scope is determined by where code is written in the source. A function resolves free variables in the scope where it was defined, regardless of where it is called.
What is variable shadowing?
