Declaring a variable in an inner scope with the same name as one in an outer scope; the inner one hides the outer within its scope.

topics.name: Closures: Practical Patterns

beginner.content:
What is a closure?

• A closure is a function together with the variables of the scope where it was created. The function keeps access to those variables even after the outer function has returned.
• Every function in JavaScript is a closure; the effect is visible when an inner function is returned or passed elsewhere.
• Closures give you private state without classes.

intermediate.content:
Common closure patterns

• Factory: a function that returns functions configured by its arguments.
• Memoization: cache results in a closed-over Map.
• Once / debounce / throttle: wrap a function with closed-over state (a flag or a timer id).
• Module pattern: an IIFE returning a public API while the rest stays private.

expert.content:
Closure bugs and memory

• Loop capture: var in a loop shares one variable between all closures; let gives each iteration its own.
• Stale closures: a callback keeps the old value of a variable it captured (a classic React hooks bug). Re-create the callback or read the latest value through a ref.
• Memory: a closure keeps its whole captured scope alive. A long-lived listener that captures a large object prevents it from being garbage-collected until the listener is removed.

interviewQA: What is a closure and where do you use it?
A function bundled with references to its surrounding scope. Use it for private state, factories, memoization, callbacks that need context, debounce/throttle and the module pattern.
Why do closures inside a var loop print the same value?
All closures share the single function-scoped var. Use let (new binding per iteration) or wrap the body in an IIFE to capture the value.
Can closures cause memory leaks?

They keep captured variables reachable. If a long-lived reference (an event listener, a timer, a global cache) holds the closure, everything it captured stays in memory until that reference is released.

topics.name: this: The Four Binding Rules

beginner.content:
What is this?

• this is decided by how a function is called, not where it is written (except for arrow functions).
• Method call obj.fn(): this is obj. Plain call fn(): this is undefined in strict mode (the global object otherwise).
• Constructor call new Fn(): this is the new object.
• Explicit: fn.call(obj, a), fn.apply(obj, [a]), fn.bind(obj) set this directly.

intermediate.content:
Arrow functions and callbacks

• Arrow functions have no own this: they use the this of the surrounding code (lexical this). Perfect for callbacks inside methods; wrong for object methods and constructors.
• Passing a method as a callback (setTimeout(obj.method, 0), button.onclick = obj.method) loses its object. Fix with bind or an arrow wrapper.
• In event handlers added with addEventListener and a normal function, this is the element.

expert.content:
Binding precedence and edge cases

• Priority: new beats explicit binding (bind/call), which beats method call, which beats plain call.
• bind returns a function whose this can not be changed again (not even by call).
• Class bodies are strict, so extracting a class method and calling it gives this === undefined. Class fields with arrows (handle = () => {}) bind per instance.
• globalThis is the portable name of the global object (window, self, global).

interviewQA: How is the value of this determined?

By the call site: new (new object), call/apply/bind (explicit), obj.method() (the object), plain call (undefined in strict mode, global otherwise). Arrow functions ignore these and use the enclosing this.
Difference between call, apply and bind?
call and apply invoke immediately; call takes arguments one by one, apply takes an array. bind returns a new function with this (and optional leading arguments) fixed.
Why shouldn't you use an arrow function as an object method?
An arrow has no own this, so inside it this is the surrounding scope's this (often undefined or window), not the object.

topics.name: Destructuring, Spread and Rest

beginner.content:
Unpacking values

• Array destructuring picks by position: const [a, b] = arr. Object destructuring picks by name: const { name, age } = user.
• Rename with { name: userName }, give defaults with { role = "guest" }, skip items with commas [, second].
• Rest (...rest) gathers the remainder; spread (...x) expands an iterable or object into place.

intermediate.content:
Destructuring in parameters and loops

• Destructure function parameters to document and default an "options object": function connect({ host = "localhost", port = 3306 } = {}).
• Use it in for...of over Object.entries or a Map: for (const [key, value] of map).
• Swap variables with [a, b] = [b, a]. Return several values from a function as an array or an object and destructure at the call site.

expert.content:
Pitfalls

• Destructuring null or undefined throws a TypeError. Default the source: const { a } = obj ?? {}.
• A default applies only for undefined, not for null.
• Spread makes shallow copies; nested objects are shared. Spreading a large array into function arguments (Math.max(...hugeArray)) can exceed the argument limit.
• Object spread copies only own enumerable properties and drops prototype methods.

interviewQA: What is the difference between spread and rest?

Both use ... . Rest collects remaining items into an array or object (in parameters and destructuring targets). Spread expands an iterable or object into individual elements (in calls, array and object literals).
When does a destructuring default apply?
Only when the value is undefined. null, 0, "" and false do not trigger the default.
Is spread a deep copy?
No. It copies the top level only; nested objects remain shared references.

topics.name: Modern Syntax: Template Literals, Optional Chaining and More

beginner.content:
ES6+ conveniences

• Template literals for interpolation and multi-line text; arrow functions for short callbacks.
• Default parameters, shorthand properties and computed keys ({ [key]: value }).
• Optional chaining ?. and nullish coalescing ?? (ES2020) remove most defensive if checks.
• Array.prototype.includes, Object.entries, padStart, Promise.allSettled, structuredClone, at(), Object.hasOwn: small additions you will use daily.

intermediate.content:
Symbols, iterators and generators

• Symbol() creates a unique key, used for hidden properties and well-known protocols (Symbol.iterator).
• An object is iterable when it has a [Symbol.iterator]() method returning { next() }. Iterables work with for...of, spread and destructuring.
• A generator (function* with yield) writes iterators as straight-line code and produces values lazily.

expert.content:
Newer language features worth knowing

• Private class fields #secret (ES2022), static blocks, top-level await in modules.
• Immutable array methods: toSorted, toReversed, with, findLast, Object.groupBy.
• Logical assignment ||= &&= ??= and numeric separators 1_000_000.
• Check browser/Node support (caniuse, MDN compat tables) and use a build step (Babel, esbuild, TypeScript) when you must support older runtimes.

interviewQA: What is optional chaining?
The ?. operator reads a property or calls a method only if the left side is not null/undefined; otherwise the whole expression becomes undefined without throwing.
What is a generator?
A function declared with function* that can pause at yield and resume later, returning an iterator. It produces values lazily and is the basis of many async patterns.
What makes an object iterable?
A [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an iterator object with a next() method returning { value, done }.

topics.name: Array Methods: map, filter, reduce and Friends

beginner.content:
Transforming arrays without loops

• map(fn) returns a new array of the same length with each item transformed.
• filter(fn) keeps the items for which fn returns truthy.
• reduce(fn, initial) folds the array into one value (a sum, an object, a new array).
• find/findIndex return the first match; some/every return a boolean; forEach just runs code and returns nothing.
codeExamples:
const products = [
  { name: "Pen", price: 10, stock: 5 },
  { name: "Book", price: 250, stock: 0 },
  { name: "Bag", price: 900, stock: 3 },
];
const names = products.map(p => p.name);                 // ["Pen", "Book", "Bag"]
const inStock = products.filter(p => p.stock > 0);        // Pen, Bag
const total = inStock.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price * p.stock, 0);
console.log(names, inStock.length, total);               // ... 2 2750

console.log(products.find(p => p.price > 100).name);      // Book
console.log(products.some(p => p.stock === 0));           // true
console.log(products.every(p => p.price > 5));            // true

intermediate.content:
Chaining and reduce as a Swiss-army knife

• Chain the methods into a readable pipeline: filter, then map, then reduce.
• reduce can group, count, index and flatten. Always pass the initial value; reducing an empty array without one throws.
• flatMap maps and flattens one level in one pass.
• sort and reverse mutate, map/filter do not. Know which is which.

expert.content:
Gotchas and performance

• ["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt) gives [1, NaN, NaN] because map passes (value, index, array) and parseInt uses the index as the radix. Use map(Number) or an arrow.
• forEach ignores returned values and promises; async callbacks in map return an array of promises (wrap with Promise.all).
• Each chained step creates an intermediate array: for huge data, a single for loop or reduce is faster.
• find stops at the first hit; filter(...)[0] scans everything.
codeExamples:
console.log(["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt));      // [1, NaN, NaN]
console.log(["1", "2", "3"].map(Number));        // [1, 2, 3]

const ids = [1, 2, 3];
const promises = ids.map(async id => id * 2);
console.log(promises[0] instanceof Promise);     // true
Promise.all(promises).then(console.log);         // [2, 4, 6]

try { [].reduce((a, b) => a + b); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); } // TypeError

interviewQA: Difference between map and forEach?
map returns a new array of the callback results and is chainable. forEach returns undefined and is used only for side effects.
What does reduce do without an initial value?
It uses the first element as the accumulator and starts at the second. On an empty array it throws a TypeError, so always provide an initial value.
Why does ["1","2","3"].map(parseInt) fail?
map calls the callback with (item, index). parseInt treats the index as the radix: parseInt("2", 1) is NaN and parseInt("3", 2) is NaN.

topics.name: Map and WeakMap

beginner.content:
Map: a real dictionary

• new Map() stores key-value pairs where keys can be any value (objects, functions, numbers), remembers insertion order and has a size.
• API: set, get, has, delete, clear, keys, values, entries, forEach. It is iterable with for...of.

intermediate.content:
Map vs Object, and conversions

• Use a Map for frequent adds/removes, non-string keys, or when you need size and order without extra code. Use an object for fixed records and JSON.
• new Map(Object.entries(obj)) and Object.fromEntries(map) convert both ways. Maps do not serialise to JSON directly.
• Map keys compare with SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and two identical-looking object literals are different keys.
• A Map is an excellent cache and counter.

expert.content:
WeakMap and private data

• A WeakMap holds its keys (objects only) weakly: if nothing else references the key, the entry is garbage-collected. It is not iterable and has no size.
• Use it to attach metadata or caches to objects you do not own (DOM nodes, framework objects) without causing memory leaks.
• It was the classic way to keep private instance data before #private fields.

interviewQA: Map vs Object?
Map: any key type, insertion-ordered, size property, better for frequent add/remove, no prototype keys. Object: string/symbol keys, JSON-friendly, literal syntax, best for fixed records.
What is a WeakMap used for?
Associating data with objects without preventing their garbage collection: metadata caches and private data. Keys must be objects and it cannot be iterated.
Can you JSON.stringify a Map?
Not directly (it yields {}). Convert first: JSON.stringify([...map]) or Object.fromEntries(map).

topics.name: Set and WeakSet

beginner.content:
Set: unique values

• A Set stores each value at most once, keeps insertion order and checks membership in roughly constant time.
• API: add, has, delete, clear, size; iterate with for...of or spread.
• The fastest way to remove duplicates: [...new Set(arr)].

intermediate.content:
Set algebra

• Set operations answer "what do these lists share?" Newer engines provide union, intersection, difference, isSubsetOf; elsewhere write them with filter.
• Use Sets for permission checks, visited-node tracking in graph algorithms and deduplicating IDs.
• Objects inside a Set are compared by reference, so new Set([{a:1},{a:1}]).size is 2.

expert.content:
WeakSet and complexity

• A WeakSet holds objects weakly: use it to mark objects as "seen" or "processed" without keeping them alive. Not iterable, no size.
• Set#has is O(1) on average, while array.includes is O(n). For repeated membership tests on big lists, convert to a Set once.
• Order of iteration is insertion order, so a Set doubles as an ordered unique list.

interviewQA: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
[...new Set(arr)] (or Array.from(new Set(arr))). For arrays of objects, dedupe by a key using a Map or Set of the key.
Why is Set.has faster than Array.includes?
A Set uses a hash table (average O(1) lookup); includes scans the array linearly (O(n)).
What is a WeakSet?
A set of objects held weakly: it does not stop them being garbage-collected, cannot be iterated and has no size. Useful for tagging objects as processed.

subTopics.name: Phase 7 · DOM Manipulation and Events (Essential for browser development)

topics.name: DOM: Selecting and Modifying Elements

beginner.content:
The Document Object Model

• The browser turns HTML into a tree of objects (the DOM). JavaScript reads and changes that tree to update the page.
• Select: document.querySelector(css) (first match) and querySelectorAll(css) (a static NodeList). getElementById is the fastest for ids.
• Change text with textContent, attributes with setAttribute/dataset, styles with classList.add/remove/toggle.
codeExamples:
Hello

  • One
  • Two
// JavaScript const title = document.getElementById("title"); title.textContent = "Welcome"; title.classList.add("highlight"); title.dataset.page = "home"; // data-page="home" const items = document.querySelectorAll("#list li"); items.forEach((li, i) => li.textContent = (i + 1) + ". " + li.textContent); const link = document.createElement("a"); link.href = "https://example.com"; link.textContent = "Visit"; document.body.append(link); // add to the page

intermediate.content:
Creating, inserting and removing nodes

• Create with createElement, insert with append, prepend, before, after, replaceWith; remove with el.remove().
• Build many nodes in a DocumentFragment and insert once, so the browser re-renders one time.
• innerHTML parses strings as HTML: fast to write but unsafe with user data and it destroys listeners on replaced nodes. Prefer textContent and DOM methods.
• Read layout (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect) and write styles in separate batches to avoid layout thrashing.

expert.content:
Live vs static collections and performance

• getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that changes as the DOM changes; querySelectorAll returns a static snapshot. Looping over a live list while adding/removing nodes can cause surprises.
• Reflow (layout) and repaint are expensive. Batch DOM writes, use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates and prefer CSS classes over many inline style writes.
• Avoid reading layout properties right after writing styles inside a loop: the browser must recompute layout each time (layout thrashing).
• MutationObserver watches changes to the tree instead of polling.

interviewQA: Difference between textContent, innerText and innerHTML?
textContent sets/reads raw text (fast, safe). innerText is layout-aware (respects CSS visibility, slower). innerHTML parses the string as HTML: powerful but an XSS risk with untrusted input.
querySelectorAll vs getElementsByClassName?
querySelectorAll accepts any CSS selector and returns a static NodeList. getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that updates automatically.
How do you avoid slow DOM updates?
Batch changes (DocumentFragment, one innerHTML/append), toggle CSS classes instead of many style writes, separate reads from writes and animate with requestAnimationFrame or CSS.

topics.name: Events: Bubbling, Capturing and Delegation

beginner.content:
Reacting to the user

• Attach a handler with element.addEventListener("click", handler); remove it with removeEventListener using the same function reference.
• The handler receives an event object: event.target (what was clicked), event.currentTarget (where the listener is), event.preventDefault() (stop the default action, e.g. form submit or link navigation).
• Common events: click, input, change, submit, keydown, focus, mouseover, DOMContentLoaded.

intermediate.content:
Bubbling, capturing and delegation

• An event travels three phases: capture (window down to the target), target, then bubble (target back up). Listeners run in the bubble phase by default.
• Event delegation: attach one listener to a parent and check event.target (use closest()). It handles items added later and saves memory.
• stopPropagation() stops bubbling; use it sparingly because it breaks other listeners and analytics.
• Options: { once: true }, { passive: true } (for scroll/touch performance), { capture: true }.

expert.content:
Custom events, memory and debouncing

• new CustomEvent("cart:add", { detail: {...}, bubbles: true }) plus dispatchEvent decouples components.
• Listeners keep their closure alive. In single-page apps remove listeners (or use AbortController: { signal }) when a component is torn down.
• Debounce waits until activity stops (search box); throttle limits the rate (scroll, resize).
• Use passive: true on scroll/touch listeners that never call preventDefault so scrolling stays smooth.

interviewQA: What is event delegation?
Putting a single listener on a common ancestor and using event.target to find which child triggered it. It works for dynamically added elements and uses fewer listeners.
Difference between event.target and event.currentTarget?
target is the innermost element that triggered the event. currentTarget is the element the running listener is attached to.
preventDefault vs stopPropagation?
preventDefault cancels the browser's default action (submit, navigation). stopPropagation stops the event from bubbling to ancestors. They are independent.

topics.name: Forms, Validation and Observers

beginner.content:
Reading form data

• new FormData(form) collects all named fields; Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)) gives a plain object.
• The browser validates attributes like required, type="email", minlength, pattern. Call form.checkValidity() or reportValidity().
• Always validate again on the server: client-side checks are for user experience only.

intermediate.content:
IntersectionObserver: lazy loading and infinite scroll

• IntersectionObserver reports when an element enters or leaves the viewport, without scroll handlers.
• Typical uses: lazy-loading images, infinite scroll, "reveal on scroll" animations and analytics for what the user actually saw.
• Call unobserve once you are done with an element.

expert.content:
MutationObserver, ResizeObserver and DOM safety

• MutationObserver reports added/removed nodes and attribute changes (watch third-party widgets, implement "wait for element").
• ResizeObserver reports element size changes (responsive components, charts) without polling.
• Sanitise any HTML string you must insert (DOMPurify) and prefer textContent; set rel="noopener noreferrer" on target="_blank" links.

interviewQA: Why validate on the server if the browser validates forms?
Client-side validation can be bypassed (devtools, curl, scripts). It improves UX but only server-side validation protects data integrity and security.
What is IntersectionObserver used for?
Detecting when elements become visible: lazy loading images, infinite scrolling and scroll-triggered animations, more efficiently than scroll event handlers.
How do you read all fields of a form?
new FormData(form), then Object.fromEntries(formData) for a plain object (multiple values with the same name need getAll).

topics.name: The Event Loop, Call Stack and Task Queues

beginner.content:
One thread, many tasks

• JavaScript runs your code on a single call stack. Long synchronous work freezes the page because nothing else can run.
• Asynchronous operations (timers, network, events) are handled by the environment (browser/Node); when they finish, their callbacks are queued.
• The event loop pushes a queued callback onto the stack only when the stack is empty.

intermediate.content:
Macrotasks and microtasks

• Macrotasks (task queue): setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events.
• Microtasks: promise callbacks (.then, await continuations), queueMicrotask, MutationObserver.
• After every macrotask, the engine drains the entire microtask queue before the next macrotask (and before rendering). So promise callbacks beat setTimeout(..., 0).

expert.content:
Starvation and keeping the UI responsive

• A promise chain that keeps scheduling new microtasks can starve rendering and timers.
• Break heavy computation into chunks (setTimeout, requestIdleCallback, scheduler.yield()) or move it to a Web Worker.
• requestAnimationFrame runs just before the next paint, the right place for visual updates.
• In Node.js the loop has phases (timers, poll, check) and process.nextTick runs before promise microtasks.

interviewQA: Output order: setTimeout 0 vs Promise.then?
The promise callback (microtask) runs first because microtasks are drained after the current task, before the next macrotask such as the timeout.
Why is JavaScript called single-threaded but non-blocking?
One call stack executes JS, but I/O and timers are performed by the host environment and their callbacks are queued and run via the event loop when the stack is empty.
What is a microtask?
A job queued by promises (then/catch/finally, await), queueMicrotask or MutationObserver, executed right after the current script/task and before the next macrotask or render.

topics.name: Promises and Combinators

beginner.content:
A promise is a value that arrives later

• A Promise is in one of three states: pending, fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with a reason). Once settled it never changes.
• Consume with .then(onFulfilled), .catch(onRejected), .finally(cleanup). Each returns a new promise, enabling chaining.
• Create with new Promise((resolve, reject) => {...}), or Promise.resolve(x) / Promise.reject(err).

intermediate.content:
Running promises together

• Promise.all([...]): waits for all; rejects as soon as one rejects.
• Promise.allSettled([...]): waits for all and reports each outcome (never rejects).
• Promise.race([...]): settles with the first promise to settle (useful for timeouts). Promise.any([...]): first fulfilled one, rejects only if all fail.
• Run independent requests in parallel with all instead of awaiting them one after another.

expert.content:
Error propagation and common mistakes

• A rejection skips .then handlers until a .catch. A thrown error inside .then becomes a rejection of the returned promise.
• Always return the inner promise inside .then, or the chain will not wait for it.
• Unhandled rejections trigger the unhandledrejection event (and crash Node by default). Every chain needs a final .catch.
• The "promise constructor anti-pattern": do not wrap something that already returns a promise in new Promise.

interviewQA: Promise.all vs allSettled?
all rejects immediately if any promise rejects and returns only fulfilled values otherwise. allSettled always waits for every promise and returns an array of {status, value|reason}.
What does .then return?
A new promise that resolves with the handler's return value (or adopts it if it is a promise) and rejects if the handler throws.
How do you implement a timeout for a promise?
Promise.race([actual, timeoutPromise]) where timeoutPromise rejects after N ms (and use AbortController to actually cancel a fetch).

topics.name: async/await Patterns: Sequential, Parallel, Retry

beginner.content:
Writing async code that reads like sync code

• An async function always returns a promise. await pauses that function until the promise settles and gives you the value, without blocking the thread.
• Use try / catch / finally for errors. await works only inside async functions or at the top level of an ES module.

intermediate.content:
Sequential vs parallel

• Awaiting inside a loop runs the calls one after another. If they are independent, start them all and then await Promise.all.
• forEach(async ...) does not wait. Use for...of with await (sequential) or map + Promise.all (parallel).
• Limit concurrency (e.g. 5 at a time) when firing hundreds of requests so you do not overload the server.

expert.content:
Retry, backoff, cancellation and ordering

• A retry helper with exponential backoff makes flaky networks tolerable. Retry only idempotent requests and only for retryable errors (network, 5xx, 429).
• Cancel obsolete work with AbortController so an old response cannot overwrite a newer one (race condition in search-as-you-type).
• for await (const x of asyncIterable) consumes async streams. Top-level await is allowed in ES modules.

interviewQA: What does an async function return?
Always a promise: the returned value becomes its fulfilment value, and a thrown error becomes its rejection.
Why is await inside a for loop sometimes slow?
Each iteration waits for the previous call, so total time is the sum. For independent calls start them together and await Promise.all.
Does await block the main thread?
No. It suspends only the async function; the rest of the program and the event loop continue, and the function resumes as a microtask when the promise settles.

subTopics.name: Phase 9 · Fetch API and REST Integration (Essential)

topics.name: Fetch: GET, POST, PUT and DELETE

beginner.content:
Talking to a REST API

• fetch(url, options) returns a promise of a Response. Read the body with response.json(), .text() or .blob() (each is itself a promise).
• REST maps HTTP verbs to actions: GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove. Status codes tell the result: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401/403 auth, 404 Not Found, 500 server error.

intermediate.content:
Always check response.ok

• fetch rejects only on network failure. A 404 or 500 still resolves, so check response.ok (status 200-299) yourself.
• Wrap this in one small helper and use it everywhere so every call handles errors the same way.
• Read the error body when the API returns details (validation messages) before throwing.

expert.content:
Query strings, headers and request types

• Build query strings with URLSearchParams, never by hand: it encodes special characters.
• Send files with FormData and do not set Content-Type yourself (the browser adds the multipart boundary).
• Conditional requests with ETag/If-None-Match and the cache option save bandwidth.
• keepalive: true lets a request outlive page unload (analytics).

interviewQA: Does fetch reject on HTTP 404 or 500?
No. It rejects only when the request cannot complete (network failure, CORS block, abort). For HTTP errors the promise resolves with response.ok === false, so you must check ok or status.
Why is response.json() asynchronous?
The body arrives as a stream. Reading and parsing it takes time, so json(), text() and blob() return promises. A body can be read only once (clone() if needed).
How do you send JSON with fetch?
method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(data).

topics.name: Timeouts, Cancellation and CORS

beginner.content:
Cancelling a request

• AbortController gives you a signal to pass to fetch. Calling controller.abort() rejects the promise with an AbortError.
• AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates a signal that aborts automatically.
• Cancel requests when a component unmounts or when a newer search supersedes an older one.

intermediate.content:
CORS: why the browser blocks your call

• Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: a page on http://localhost:5173 cannot read a response from http://localhost:3001 unless that server allows it with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
• "Non-simple" requests (JSON content type, custom headers, PUT/DELETE) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request first.
• Fix CORS on the server (or proxy through the dev server). In Spring Boot use @CrossOrigin or a global CorsConfigurationSource; allow only your own origins.
• Sending cookies cross-origin needs credentials: "include" on the client and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true plus an explicit (not *) origin on the server.

expert.content:
Authentication and robust clients

• Send tokens in the Authorization: Bearer ... header. Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies for session tokens so JavaScript (and therefore XSS) cannot read them.
• Handle 401 centrally: refresh the token once, retry the request, otherwise redirect to login.
• Add retries with backoff for idempotent calls only; show loading and error states in the UI; debounce search requests.
• Validate and normalise API data at the boundary (a schema library such as Zod) so bad responses fail early with a clear message.

interviewQA: What is CORS and who fixes it?
A browser security rule that blocks cross-origin reads unless the server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-* headers. The fix is on the server (or via a dev proxy), not in client JavaScript.
What is a preflight request?
An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before a non-simple cross-origin request to ask whether the real method and headers are allowed.
How do you cancel a fetch?
Pass an AbortSignal from an AbortController (or AbortSignal.timeout) and call abort(); the promise rejects with AbortError.

topics.name: Mini Project: REST Client for a Spring Boot API

beginner.content:
What we are building

• A small "tasks" page that lists, adds, completes and deletes tasks through a Spring Boot REST API (GET /api/tasks, POST /api/tasks, PATCH /api/tasks/{id}, DELETE /api/tasks/{id}).
• It puts together fetch, async/await, error handling, DOM rendering and event delegation from the earlier phases.
codeExamples: // app.js const list = document.querySelector("#tasks"); const status = document.querySelector("#status"); async function api(path, options) { const res = await fetch("/api/tasks" + path, { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, ...options, }); if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Request failed: " + res.status); return res.status === 204 ? null : res.json(); }

intermediate.content:
Rendering and events

• Render from data with DOM methods (textContent), keep a single render(tasks) function and call it after every change.
• Use event delegation on the list for the complete and delete buttons.
• Show a status message while loading and when something fails.

expert.content:
The Spring Boot side and improvements

• The controller returns JSON and proper status codes (201 Created with a Location header, 204 for delete, 404 when missing); validate input with @Valid.
• Improve the client: optimistic updates (update the UI first, roll back on failure), debounced search, pagination via ?page=&size=, and a retry button on errors.
• Keep API paths in one place so a base-URL change is a one-line edit.

interviewQA: What are optimistic updates?
Updating the UI immediately assuming the request will succeed, then rolling back (and informing the user) if it fails. It makes the app feel instant.
Which status code should a successful POST that creates a resource return?
201 Created, with a Location header pointing to the new resource; 200 is acceptable but less precise.
Why use textContent instead of innerHTML when rendering API data?
API data may contain user-supplied text. textContent treats it as plain text, preventing HTML/script injection (XSS).

topics.name: Prototypes and the Prototype Chain

beginner.content:
Objects inherit from objects

• Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype. When a property is not found on the object, JavaScript looks it up the prototype chain until it reaches null.
• Read the link with Object.getPrototypeOf(obj). Create an object with a chosen prototype using Object.create(proto).
• Methods placed on a shared prototype exist once in memory, instead of being copied into every object.

intermediate.content:
Constructor functions and the prototype property

• A function used with new builds an object whose prototype is Fn.prototype.
• Put methods on Fn.prototype so all instances share them; put per-instance data on this in the constructor.
• instanceof checks whether Fn.prototype appears in the object's chain.
• Chain constructors for inheritance with Object.setPrototypeOf or Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype) (the ES6 class extends syntax does this for you).

expert.content:
Pitfalls and performance

• Never mutate built-in prototypes (Array.prototype.myMethod = ...): it can clash with future language features and with other libraries.
• for...in also lists inherited enumerable properties; filter with Object.hasOwn.
• Reassigning __proto__ at runtime deoptimises engines. Set the prototype at creation time instead.
• Property lookup walks the chain: very deep chains cost a little time; engines cache lookups with hidden classes (inline caches).

interviewQA: What is the prototype chain?
The linked list of objects searched when a property is not found on the object itself: obj, then obj.[[Prototype]], and so on until null.
Difference between __proto__ and prototype?

__proto__ (properly Object.getPrototypeOf) is the actual link of an object to its prototype. prototype is a property of constructor functions: the object that becomes the [[Prototype]] of instances created with new.
Why put methods on the prototype?
All instances share one copy instead of each carrying its own function, saving memory and allowing changes to propagate.

topics.name: Classes: Fields, Getters, Static and Inheritance

beginner.content:
Class syntax

• class is syntax over prototypes: the constructor initialises instances; other methods live on the prototype.
• extends creates a subclass; super(...) calls the parent constructor (must run before touching this), super.method() calls a parent method.
• static members belong to the class, not instances. Classes are not hoisted like functions and must be called with new.

intermediate.content:
Encapsulation with # private fields

• Names starting with # are truly private: not accessible outside the class body, not even via bracket notation.
• Use getters/setters to validate on write; static #count and static {} blocks for class-level state.
• Class fields can be arrow functions (handle = () => {}) to keep this bound to the instance, handy for callbacks.

expert.content:
Composition over inheritance and mixins

• Deep inheritance trees are brittle. Prefer composition: give an object collaborators it delegates to ("has-a" instead of "is-a").
• A mixin adds behaviour to a class without a shared parent: const Serializable = Base => class extends Base {...}.
• SOLID in JavaScript: small single-purpose classes, depend on behaviour (duck typing) rather than concrete types, extend by adding, not editing.
• Use Symbol.toPrimitive, toJSON and instanceof customisation (Symbol.hasInstance) sparingly.

interviewQA: Are JavaScript classes real classes?

They are syntax sugar over prototype-based inheritance. The class keyword creates a constructor function and puts methods on its prototype, with stricter rules (must use new, always strict mode, not hoisted usable).
What does super() do?
In a constructor it calls the parent constructor and must run before this is used. super.method() calls the parent's version of a method.
Composition vs inheritance?
Inheritance models "is-a" and couples a child to its parent. Composition assembles behaviour from collaborators ("has-a"), which is more flexible and easier to test.

topics.name: ES Modules: import, export and Dynamic import

beginner.content:
Splitting code into files

• A module is a file with its own scope. Share things with export and use them with import.
• Named exports (export const x) are imported with braces and the same name; a file may have one default export imported with any name.
• In the browser load a module with <script type="module" src="main.js">. Modules are strict mode and deferred by default.

intermediate.content:
Live bindings, dynamic import and re-exports

• Imports are live read-only views of the exporting module's variables, not copies; the importer cannot assign to them.
• import("./chart.js") loads a module on demand and returns a promise: code splitting and lazy loading.
• Re-export to build a clean public API: export { Button } from "./Button.js" in an index.js barrel file.
• A module is evaluated once and cached, so module-level state acts as a singleton.

expert.content:
Bundlers, CommonJS and circular dependencies

• Node historically used CommonJS (require/module.exports); modern Node supports ES modules with "type": "module" or .mjs.
• Bundlers (Vite, esbuild, webpack) resolve bare imports (import React from "react"), tree-shake unused exports and split code into chunks.
• Circular imports can produce undefined or TDZ errors because a module sees an unfinished module. Break cycles by extracting shared code into a third module.
• Prefer named exports: they refactor better and enable tree-shaking and auto-imports.

interviewQA: Named export vs default export?
Named exports are imported by their exact name (many per file); a default export is one value imported under any name. Named exports are easier to tree-shake and refactor.
Are ES module imports copies?
No, they are live bindings to the exported variable; changes in the exporting module are visible, and the importing side cannot reassign them.
How do you lazy-load code?
Dynamic import(): const mod = await import("./heavy.js"). Bundlers turn it into a separate chunk fetched on demand.

topics.name: Error Handling: try/catch, Custom Errors, Global Handlers

beginner.content:
try / catch / finally

• Code that may throw goes in try; catch (err) handles it; finally always runs (close files, hide spinners).
• Throw Error objects, not strings: they carry a name, message and a stack trace.
• Built-in types: TypeError, RangeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError. JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on bad input.

intermediate.content:
Custom errors and the cause chain

• Extend Error for domain errors so callers can react with instanceof: ValidationError, NotFoundError, HttpError.
• Attach structured data (status code, field name) as properties.
• Wrap low-level errors without losing the original using new Error("message", { cause: err }).
• Handle errors where you can do something useful; otherwise let them propagate. Do not swallow errors with an empty catch.

expert.content:
Global safety nets and async errors

• window.onerror / addEventListener("error") catches uncaught exceptions; "unhandledrejection" catches unhandled promise rejections. Use them to log to a monitoring service (Sentry), not to hide problems.
• try/catch does not catch errors thrown inside callbacks that run later (setTimeout) unless the try is inside that callback; with async/await it works as expected.
• In React, an error boundary catches render errors. In Express, use an error-handling middleware with four parameters.
• Show friendly messages to users; log technical details (stack, request id) separately.

interviewQA: Does finally run after return inside try?
Yes. finally always runs after try/catch, even if try returns or throws; a return in finally overrides the earlier return.
Why does try/catch not catch an error in setTimeout?
The callback runs later on a different call stack, after the try block has finished. Put try/catch inside the callback or use async/await.
What is error.cause?
An option (ES2022) to chain errors: new Error("high-level message", { cause: lowLevelError }), preserving the original error for debugging.

topics.name: Debugging: DevTools, Console and Breakpoints

beginner.content:
Beyond console.log

• console.log variants: console.table(array) for tabular data, console.error/warn, console.group, console.dir(obj), console.assert(cond, msg), console.trace() for the call path.
• console.time("label") / console.timeEnd("label") measure code.
• Logging { variable } instead of variable prints the name too.

intermediate.content:
Breakpoints and the debugger

• Open DevTools (F12) → Sources. Click a line number for a breakpoint; execution pauses there and you can inspect the Scope, Call Stack and Watch panels.
• Step controls: Step over (F10), Step into (F11), Step out (Shift+F11), Resume (F8).
• The debugger; statement pauses when DevTools is open. Conditional breakpoints pause only when an expression is true; logpoints log without editing code.
• Use Pause on exceptions to stop at the line that throws.

expert.content:
Network, performance and memory debugging

• Network tab: check the request URL, status, payload, response, headers and timing; throttle to "Slow 3G" to test real conditions; "Preserve log" across navigations.
• Performance tab: record, then look for long tasks (red corners) and layout thrashing. Lighthouse audits speed and accessibility.
• Memory tab: take heap snapshots before and after an action; objects that keep growing and are retained by listeners or globals are leaks.
• Source maps let you debug the original TypeScript/JSX instead of the minified bundle. In Node: node --inspect-brk app.js and attach the DevTools or VS Code debugger.

interviewQA: How do you debug JavaScript in the browser?
Use DevTools: Console for logs/errors, Sources for breakpoints and stepping, Network for requests, Performance and Memory for speed and leaks. The debugger; statement also pauses execution.
What is a source map?
A file mapping minified/transpiled code back to the original source so DevTools shows readable code and line numbers.
console.log vs a breakpoint?
console.log is quick but static and needs code edits. A breakpoint pauses execution so you can inspect all variables, the call stack and step through logic interactively.

subTopics.name: Phase 12 · Browser APIs and Web Storage (Important)

topics.name: Web Storage: localStorage, sessionStorage, Cookies, IndexedDB

beginner.content:
Storing data in the browser

• localStorage: key-value strings (about 5 MB), persists until cleared, shared by tabs of the same origin. sessionStorage: the same, but per tab and cleared when it closes.
• Values are always strings, so use JSON.stringify / JSON.parse for objects. The API is synchronous, so keep it small.
• Methods: setItem, getItem (returns null if missing), removeItem, clear.

intermediate.content:
Safe usage and cookies

• Wrap storage access in try/catch: it can throw in private mode, when the quota is full or when storage is blocked.
• Never store secrets (passwords, access tokens) in localStorage: any XSS can read it. Prefer HttpOnly cookies set by the server.
• Cookies are sent with every request to the server; set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax|Strict. Keep them small.
• Version your stored data and handle missing/old shapes.

expert.content:
IndexedDB and the Cache API

• IndexedDB is an asynchronous, transactional database for large structured data (hundreds of MB), blobs and offline apps. Use a wrapper like idb or Dexie to avoid the verbose event API.
• The Cache API with a service worker stores responses so a progressive web app works offline.
• Check quota with navigator.storage.estimate(); request persistence with navigator.storage.persist().
• Choose: preference flag → localStorage; large/offline data → IndexedDB; auth → HttpOnly cookie.

interviewQA: localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?
localStorage persists across sessions per origin; sessionStorage lasts for one tab; cookies are small, can expire, and are automatically sent to the server with each request (and can be HttpOnly).
Is localStorage safe for JWTs?
It is readable by any script on the page, so an XSS attack can steal the token. Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, or keep short-lived tokens in memory.
When would you use IndexedDB?
For large or structured offline data, queries by index and binary data, where the synchronous 5 MB string-only localStorage is not enough.

topics.name: Useful Browser APIs: History, URL, Clipboard, Geolocation, Intl

beginner.content:
Navigation and URLs

• new URL(href) parses a URL into searchParams, pathname, hash. Read the current page with location.
• The History API (history.pushState, popstate) changes the address bar without a reload: the foundation of single-page-app routers.
• location.assign() navigates; location.replace() navigates without adding a history entry.

intermediate.content:
Clipboard, Geolocation, Notifications, Share

• Many APIs need HTTPS, a user gesture and/or permission, and return promises. Always handle denial.
• navigator.clipboard.writeText() copies text; navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition() reads the position; Notification.requestPermission(); navigator.share() opens the native share sheet on mobile.
• Feature-detect before using: if ("geolocation" in navigator).

expert.content:
Intl, Web Workers, Fetch alternatives and observers

• Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.RelativeTimeFormat and Intl.PluralRules format for the user's locale. Do not hand-roll currency or date formatting.
• Web Workers run scripts on another thread (no DOM access) and talk via postMessage.
• BroadcastChannel messages other tabs; WebSocket and Server-Sent Events give real-time updates; requestAnimationFrame syncs animations with the screen.
• Use structuredClone to copy data safely between contexts.

interviewQA: How do single-page apps change the URL without reloading?
With the History API: history.pushState/replaceState update the URL and a popstate listener reacts to back/forward; the router then renders the matching view.
Why are some browser APIs only available on HTTPS?
Powerful features (clipboard, geolocation, service workers, camera) are restricted to secure contexts so that network attackers cannot abuse them. localhost is treated as secure for development.
What is a Web Worker for?
Running heavy JavaScript on a separate thread so the UI stays responsive. Workers have no DOM access and communicate through postMessage.

subTopics.name: Phase 13 · Security and Testing (Essential for production)

topics.name: Web Security: XSS, CSRF, CSP and Safe Coding

beginner.content:
Cross-site scripting (XSS)

• XSS happens when untrusted text is inserted into the page as HTML or script. The attacker's script then runs with the user's privileges (reads storage, calls APIs, steals sessions).
• Types: stored (saved in the database and shown to others), reflected (echoed from the URL), DOM-based (client-side code writes input into the DOM).
• Defence: output-encode by default. Use textContent instead of innerHTML; frameworks like React escape automatically.

intermediate.content:
CSRF, CSP and cookies

• CSRF: another site makes the user's browser send an authenticated request (cookies go along automatically). Defences: SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies, CSRF tokens, checking Origin, requiring a custom header for JSON APIs.
• Content-Security-Policy (response header) restricts where scripts can load from and blocks inline scripts, limiting the damage of XSS.
• Session cookies: HttpOnly (not readable by JS), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite.
• Serve everything over HTTPS and use rel="noopener noreferrer" on external target="_blank" links.

expert.content:
Secure coding checklist

• Never trust input: validate type, length and format on the client for UX and again on the server for safety. Use allow-lists.
• Do not use eval, new Function, document.write or setTimeout("string"); avoid innerHTML with dynamic data.
• Beware prototype pollution: merging untrusted JSON into objects with keys like __proto__ or constructor. Use Object.create(null), Map, or validate keys.
• Keep dependencies updated (npm audit), pin versions with a lockfile and use Subresource Integrity (integrity="sha384-...") for CDN scripts.
• Do not put secrets (API keys with write access) in front-end code; anything shipped to the browser is public.

interviewQA: How do you prevent XSS?

Treat all data as untrusted: render with textContent or a framework that escapes, sanitise any HTML you must allow (DOMPurify), set a Content-Security-Policy, and use HttpOnly cookies so stolen scripts cannot read sessions.
What is CSRF and how is it prevented?
A malicious site makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request to your site. Prevent with SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, Origin checks and not using GET for state changes.
What is prototype pollution?
Injecting properties into Object.prototype by merging attacker-controlled keys such as __proto__, which then appear on every object and can bypass checks like isAdmin.

topics.name: Testing: Unit Tests, Mocks and Test-Driven Development

beginner.content:
Why and what to test

• Automated tests catch regressions and make refactoring safe. The testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a few end-to-end tests.
• Popular runners: Vitest (Vite projects), Jest, and the built-in node:test. Each test follows Arrange, Act, Assert.
• Test behaviour (inputs and outputs), not implementation details.

intermediate.content:
Mocks, spies and async tests

• A mock replaces a dependency (network, database, clock) so the unit is tested alone and deterministically. A spy records how a function was called.
• Mock fetch or the module that wraps it; use fake timers for setTimeout/debounce.
• Async tests await the result (or return the promise) and assert on resolves/rejects.

expert.content:
Component, end-to-end tests and TDD

• Component tests (Testing Library) render a component and interact with it like a user: find by role/text, click, assert on visible output.
• End-to-end tests (Playwright, Cypress) drive a real browser through whole flows such as login and checkout. Keep them few and stable.
• TDD: write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest code, then refactor. Measure coverage, but treat it as a guide, not a goal.
• Run tests in CI on every push; a failing test should block the merge.

interviewQA: What is the difference between a mock and a spy?
A spy wraps a real function to record calls while (optionally) running it; a mock replaces the dependency entirely with controlled behaviour and expectations.
What is the testing pyramid?
Many fast, isolated unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle and a small number of slow end-to-end tests at the top.
What does test-driven development involve?
Red-green-refactor: write a failing test, write the minimum code to pass it, then clean up the code while keeping the tests green.

subTopics.name: Phase 14 · TypeScript (Essential for your chosen stack)

topics.name: TypeScript Basics: Types, Interfaces and Unions

beginner.content:
JavaScript with a type checker

• TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript. The compiler (tsc) finds mistakes before the code runs, then removes the types, leaving plain JavaScript.
• Annotate with a colon: let age: number. Most types are inferred, so annotate function parameters and public APIs and let the rest infer.
• Basic types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, arrays number[], tuples [string, number], and any (turns checking off: avoid), unknown (safe "anything"), never.

intermediate.content:
Interfaces, type aliases, unions and narrowing

• interface and type describe object shapes. Mark optional properties with ? and immutable ones with readonly.
• A union string | number allows several types; literal types ("GET" | "POST") restrict values.
• Narrowing: typeof, instanceof, in and equality checks make the compiler refine a union inside a branch.
• A discriminated union (a shared kind field) gives exhaustive, safe switch statements.

expert.content:
Strictness and the type system's limits

• Enable "strict": true in tsconfig.json (includes strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny). It is the single most valuable setting.
• Types exist only at compile time. Data from the network, localStorage or JSON.parse is not checked at runtime: validate it (Zod, Valibot) and derive the type from the schema.
• Avoid type assertions (value as User) and non-null assertions (x!) except where you know more than the compiler; they silence errors rather than fix them.
• enum compiles to runtime code; many teams prefer union literals or as const objects.

interviewQA: What is the difference between any and unknown?
any disables type checking for that value. unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow it (typeof, instanceof, schema validation) before using it, so it stays type-safe.
interface vs type?
Both describe shapes. interface can be extended and merged (declaration merging) and suits object contracts; type can also express unions, tuples, mapped and conditional types.
Does TypeScript check types at runtime?
No. Types are erased during compilation. Validate external data at runtime (Zod etc.) to get safety at the boundaries.

topics.name: Generics, Utility Types and Type Guards

beginner.content:
Generics: reusable typed code

• A generic is a type parameter: function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined. The caller's type flows through, so you avoid any and duplication.
• Constrain with extends: <T extends { id: number }>.
• Generic interfaces describe containers such as ApiResponse<T>, Promise<T> and Array<T>.

intermediate.content:
Built-in utility types

• Partial<T> (all optional), Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, Record<K, V>, ReturnType<F>, Awaited<T>.
• Use them to derive related types instead of copy-pasting: a "create" payload is Omit<User, "id">; a patch is Partial<User>.
• Mapped and conditional types build new types from old ones (keyof T, T[K], T extends U ? X : Y).

expert.content:
Type guards and declaration files

• A type guard is a function returning value is Type; after it returns true, the compiler narrows the type.
• satisfies checks a value against a type without widening it.
• Libraries without types ship or need declaration files (.d.ts, @types/xyz). Declare your own with declare module.
• Prefer unknown in catch blocks (useUnknownInCatchVariables) and narrow with instanceof Error.

interviewQA: What are generics?
Type parameters that let a function, class or interface work with many types while keeping type information (function first<T>(a: T[]): T).
What do Partial, Pick and Omit do?
Partial makes all properties optional, Pick selects some properties, Omit removes some. They derive new types from existing ones so you do not duplicate definitions.
What is a type guard?
A runtime check (typeof, instanceof, in, or a function returning "x is T") that tells the compiler to narrow a union to a specific type inside a branch.

topics.name: TypeScript Tooling: tsconfig, Build and React

beginner.content:
Project setup

• npm i -D typescript then npx tsc --init creates tsconfig.json. Key options: target, module, strict, outDir, rootDir, noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
• tsc --noEmit type-checks only; modern bundlers (Vite, esbuild) strip types without checking, so run tsc --noEmit in CI as the type gate.
• Use .ts for logic and .tsx for files with JSX.

intermediate.content:
Typing React components and events

• Type props with an interface; React.ReactNode for children; useState<User | null>(null) to give state a union type.
• Event types: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.FormEvent, React.MouseEvent.
• Generic components (function List<T>(props: { items: T[]; render: (item: T) => ReactNode })) keep type safety across reusable pieces.

expert.content:
Migrating a JavaScript project

• Migrate gradually: add "allowJs": true and "checkJs": false, rename files one by one to .ts, fix errors, then turn on strict options one at a time.
• Start with the types of your domain objects and API responses; the rest follows through inference.
• Use ESLint with typescript-eslint for rules the compiler does not cover (floating promises, unsafe any).
• Share types between front end and back end by generating them from an OpenAPI spec (for a Spring Boot API: springdoc plus openapi-typescript).

interviewQA: Why run tsc --noEmit if Vite already builds the project?
Vite/esbuild only strip types and do not type-check. tsc --noEmit is the step that actually reports type errors, so it belongs in CI and in the build script.
What does strict mode enable?
A group of checks including strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes and strictPropertyInitialization, catching the most common bugs such as null/undefined access.
How do you get types for a library with no types?
Install @types/<name> from DefinitelyTyped, or write a declaration file (declare module "lib";) with the parts you use.

subTopics.name: Phase 15 · React (Essential for your chosen stack)

topics.name: React Components, Props and State

beginner.content:
Thinking in components

• React builds the UI from components: functions that take props (inputs) and return JSX (a description of the UI).
• The UI is a function of state: when state changes, React re-renders the component and updates only the changed DOM.
• JSX rules: one root element (or a fragment <>...</>), className instead of class, { } to embed JavaScript, camelCase event props like onClick.

intermediate.content:
State with useState

• const [value, setValue] = useState(initial) keeps a value between renders. Calling the setter schedules a re-render.
• Never mutate state: create a new array/object ([...items, item], {...user, name}) so React sees the change.
• When the new state depends on the old, use the functional form: setCount(c => c + 1).
• Lift state up to the nearest common parent when two components need the same data; pass it down as props and pass callbacks to change it.

expert.content:
Rendering rules and keys

• Components must be pure during render: no mutation of props/state, no network calls. Side effects belong in event handlers and useEffect.
• Keys identify list items between renders. Use stable ids, not array indexes, when the list can reorder, insert or delete; otherwise state sticks to the wrong row.
• State updates are batched and asynchronous: reading the state right after setX still gives the old value in that render.
• Changing a component's key resets its state, a handy trick to reinitialise a form.

interviewQA: What are props and state?
Props are read-only inputs passed from a parent. State is data owned by a component that can change over time and triggers a re-render when updated.
Why do lists need keys?
Keys let React match items between renders so it can reorder, add and remove DOM nodes correctly and preserve each item's state. Use stable unique ids, not indexes, for dynamic lists.
Why use setCount(c => c + 1)?
Because state updates are batched and the closure holds the old value; the functional form always receives the latest state, so multiple updates accumulate correctly.

topics.name: Hooks: useEffect, useMemo, useRef and Custom Hooks

beginner.content:
useEffect: synchronising with the outside world

• useEffect(fn, deps) runs after render. With [] it runs once after mount; with [a, b] it re-runs when a or b change; with no array it runs after every render.
• Return a cleanup function to remove listeners, clear timers or abort requests; it runs before the next effect and on unmount.
• Typical uses: fetching data, subscriptions, timers, document title. Do not use effects to compute values from props/state: compute them during render.

intermediate.content:
useRef, useMemo and useCallback

• useRef holds a mutable value that does not trigger re-renders and gives access to DOM nodes (ref.current), e.g. focusing an input or storing the latest callback.
• useMemo(() => expensive(a), [a]) caches a computed value; useCallback(fn, deps) caches a function so memoised children (React.memo) do not re-render needlessly.
• Measure before optimising: memoisation has its own cost and most renders are cheap.
• useReducer manages complex state transitions; useContext shares values (theme, user) without prop drilling.

expert.content:
Custom hooks and the rules of hooks

• A custom hook is a function starting with use that calls other hooks. It extracts reusable stateful logic (data fetching, form handling, local storage, debouncing).
• Rules: call hooks only at the top level of components/hooks (not in loops, conditions or nested functions) and only from React functions. The linter plugin eslint-plugin-react-hooks enforces them and checks dependency arrays.
• Stale closures: an effect or callback keeps the values from the render it was created in. List every reactive value in the dependency array or use the functional setter / a ref.
• In development StrictMode mounts effects twice to expose missing cleanup. That is intentional.

interviewQA: What does the dependency array of useEffect do?
It lists the reactive values the effect uses. React re-runs the effect when any of them changes ([] means only after mount). Missing dependencies cause stale values.
useMemo vs useCallback?
useMemo caches the result of a computation; useCallback caches a function definition (equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps)). Both only help when referential equality or expensive work matters.
Why are hooks not allowed inside conditions?
React identifies each hook by its call order on every render. Conditional calls change the order and corrupt the state mapping.

topics.name: React in Practice: Data Fetching, Routing, Forms and Performance

beginner.content:
Routing and forms

• Single-page apps use a client-side router (React Router): <Routes>, <Route path="/users/:id">, useParams, useNavigate, <Link> (never a plain <a href> for internal links).
• Controlled inputs keep their value in state; uncontrolled inputs use refs/FormData. Libraries (React Hook Form with Zod) reduce boilerplate and handle validation and errors.

intermediate.content:
Server state and global state

• Server state (data owned by the API) is best handled by TanStack Query or SWR: caching, request de-duplication, background refresh, retries, loading/error states and mutations with cache invalidation.
• Client state: keep it local when possible; lift it up when shared; use Context for rarely changing values (theme, auth user); use Zustand or Redux Toolkit for large, frequently updated shared state.
• Avoid duplicating server data into useState; derive what you can during render.

expert.content:
Performance and architecture

• Re-renders are normal and cheap. Fix measured problems with the React DevTools Profiler: React.memo, useMemo/useCallback, list virtualisation (react-window) and moving state closer to where it is used.
• Code-split routes with React.lazy and <Suspense> so users download only what they open.
• Error boundaries catch render errors in a subtree and show a fallback instead of a blank page.
• Structure by feature (features/tasks/{components,hooks,api}), keep components small and test them with Testing Library.

interviewQA: Controlled vs uncontrolled components?
A controlled input's value lives in React state and is set through the value prop with an onChange handler. An uncontrolled input keeps its own DOM state and you read it through a ref or FormData.
Why use a library like TanStack Query for API data?
It provides caching, de-duplication, background refetching, retries, loading and error states and cache invalidation after mutations, which you would otherwise rebuild by hand with useEffect.
What is code splitting in React?
Loading parts of the app on demand with React.lazy and dynamic import(), wrapped in Suspense, so the initial bundle stays small.

subTopics.name: Phase 16 · Node.js and Express (Optional with Spring Boot)

topics.name: Node.js Basics: Runtime, Modules, Files and Streams

beginner.content:
JavaScript outside the browser

• Node.js runs JavaScript on the V8 engine with a non-blocking, event-driven I/O model (libuv). It has no DOM or window, but offers fs, path, http, os, crypto, process.
• npm installs packages (package.json, package-lock.json, node_modules). Use "type": "module" for ES modules.
• Command-line arguments: process.argv; environment variables: process.env.

intermediate.content:
Files, async I/O and JSON

• Prefer the promise API: import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises". Avoid the ...Sync versions in servers because they block the event loop.
• Always pass an encoding ("utf8") to get a string rather than a Buffer; resolve paths relative to the module with import.meta.url.
• Read configuration from environment variables (and a .env file during development with --env-file or dotenv), never hard-code secrets.

expert.content:
Streams, events and worker threads

• Streams process data in chunks, so a 5 GB file never has to fit in memory. Connect them with pipeline (it handles errors and cleanup).
• Many Node objects are EventEmitters: emitter.on("event", handler), emit.
• CPU-heavy work blocks the single JS thread: use worker_threads, a job queue, or run it in another service. Scale across cores with the cluster module or a process manager (PM2) and a load balancer.

interviewQA: Why is Node.js good for I/O-heavy apps?
Its non-blocking, event-driven model lets one thread serve many concurrent connections while waiting for I/O, with low memory per connection.
Why avoid fs.readFileSync in a server?
Synchronous calls block the event loop, freezing every other request until the file is read. Use the async or promise-based API.
What is a stream?
An abstraction for processing data piece by piece (read, write, transform), allowing large files or network data to be handled with constant memory and backpressure.

topics.name: Express: Routing, Middleware and a REST API

beginner.content:
A minimal server

• Express is a small web framework on top of Node's http module. A route maps a method and path to a handler (req, res).
• Parse JSON bodies with express.json(). Read req.params (path), req.query (query string), req.body; reply with res.json() and res.status().

intermediate.content:
Middleware

• Middleware are functions (req, res, next) that run in order: logging, authentication, validation, CORS, rate limiting, compression. Call next() to continue, or send a response to stop.
• An error-handling middleware has four parameters (err, req, res, next) and goes last. In Express 5 rejected promises from async handlers reach it automatically; in Express 4 wrap handlers or call next(err).
• Useful packages: helmet (security headers), cors, morgan (logs), express-rate-limit.

expert.content:
Structure, database and production

• Layer the code: routes (HTTP) → controllers/services (business logic) → repositories (database). Validate input with Zod/Joi at the edge.
• Use a real database with a driver or ORM (mysql2, Prisma) and parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection.
• Production: set NODE_ENV=production, run behind a reverse proxy (nginx) with HTTPS, handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, log structured JSON, add health endpoints.
• Node vs Spring Boot: Node/Express is quick to start and shares language and types with the front end; Spring Boot gives a mature ecosystem, strong typing, transactions and multi-threaded CPU work. If your team already uses Spring Boot, keep Node for tooling, BFF layers or real-time features.

interviewQA: What is middleware in Express?
A function (req, res, next) in the request pipeline. It can read or change the request/response, end the cycle or pass control on with next(). Order matters.
How do you prevent SQL injection in Node?
Use parameterised queries or prepared statements (placeholders) so user input is never concatenated into the SQL string; validate input as a second layer.
When would you choose Node/Express over Spring Boot?

For lightweight APIs, backend-for-frontend layers, real-time features (WebSockets) and when sharing code/types with a JavaScript front end matters. Spring Boot suits large, transactional, enterprise back ends.

topics.name: Inside the Engine: V8, JIT, Hidden Classes and Garbage Collection

beginner.content:
How JavaScript actually runs

• Engines (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) parse source into an AST, compile to bytecode and start interpreting immediately (Ignition in V8).
• Hot code is optimised to machine code by the JIT compiler (TurboFan) using type feedback from earlier runs. If an assumption breaks (a variable suddenly changes type) the code deoptimises back to bytecode.
• Practical meaning: write code with stable types and shapes and the engine makes it fast.

intermediate.content:
Hidden classes and inline caches

• V8 gives objects a hidden class (shape) describing their properties. Objects created with the same properties in the same order share a shape, so property access becomes a fast fixed-offset read cached at the call site (inline cache).
• Keep shapes consistent: initialise all properties in the constructor in the same order; do not add or delete properties later (delete can switch an object to slow dictionary mode); do not mix property order between objects.
• Arrays are fastest when homogeneous (all small integers, all doubles, all objects) and dense (no holes).

expert.content:
Garbage collection

• V8's collector is generational: new objects live in a small "young generation" that is cleaned quickly and often (scavenge); survivors move to the "old generation" cleaned by a mark-and-compact collector, largely concurrent and incremental to avoid long pauses.
• An object is collected when it is unreachable from the roots (global object, stack, active closures). You cannot free memory by hand; you remove references.
• Reduce GC pressure: avoid allocating inside hot loops, reuse buffers/objects (object pools) for tight loops, and prefer typed arrays for numeric data.
• WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry exist but are non-deterministic: never rely on them for correctness.

interviewQA: What is JIT compilation?
Just-in-time compilation: the engine starts with an interpreter, profiles running code and compiles hot paths to optimised machine code at runtime, deoptimising if its type assumptions fail.
What are hidden classes?
Internal shapes V8 assigns to objects with the same property layout, letting property access be a fast cached offset lookup. Consistent property order and no deletes keep objects on the fast path.
How does garbage collection decide what to free?
It marks everything reachable from the roots (stack, globals, closures) and frees what is not. Generational collection cleans short-lived objects quickly and long-lived ones less often.

topics.name: Memory Leaks: Finding and Fixing Them

beginner.content:
What a leak is in a garbage-collected language

• A leak is memory you no longer need but that is still reachable, so the collector cannot free it. Symptoms: the tab or process grows over time, slows down and eventually crashes.
• Common causes: forgotten timers and listeners, global variables and caches that never shrink, detached DOM nodes still referenced from JavaScript, closures capturing large objects.

intermediate.content:
Fixes

• Clean up: clearInterval, removeEventListener (keep the function reference) or AbortController signals; do it in useEffect cleanup or disconnectedCallback.
• Bound caches: use an LRU with a max size, or WeakMap/WeakRef keyed by objects.
• Drop references to DOM nodes you removed; avoid storing elements in global arrays.
• Scope variables narrowly so closures capture only what they need.

expert.content:
Finding a leak with DevTools

• Open Memory → take a heap snapshot, perform the suspect action several times, take another snapshot and compare ("Objects allocated between snapshots"). Look at Detached DOM trees and the retainers path to see what holds an object.
• The Performance tab with the Memory option shows the JS heap sawtooth: if the baseline after each GC keeps rising, you leak.
• Node: node --inspect and the same DevTools, or process.memoryUsage() and heap dumps (v8.writeHeapSnapshot()).
• Reproduce, fix, re-measure. Add a regression check for long-running pages.

interviewQA: What causes memory leaks in JavaScript?
Unremoved event listeners and timers, unbounded global caches, references to detached DOM nodes, and closures holding large objects: anything that stays reachable after it is no longer needed.
How do you find a memory leak?
Compare heap snapshots before and after repeating an action in the Memory tab, inspect retainers of growing or detached objects, and watch the post-GC heap baseline in the Performance panel.
What is a WeakRef good for?
Holding a reference that does not prevent garbage collection, for caches of expensive objects that may be rebuilt. Its behaviour is non-deterministic, so never depend on it for correctness.

topics.name: Performance: Debounce, Throttle, Virtualisation and Web Vitals

beginner.content:
Measure first

• Use Lighthouse and the DevTools Performance tab; track Core Web Vitals: LCP (largest contentful paint, loading), INP (interaction to next paint, responsiveness) and CLS (layout shift, stability).
• Instrument code with performance.now(), performance.mark/measure and the PerformanceObserver.
• Optimise the biggest bottleneck first; most slowness is network, images and too much JavaScript, not a clever loop.

intermediate.content:
Throttle, debounce and scheduling

• Debounce: run after events stop for N ms (search box, auto-save). Throttle: run at most once every N ms (scroll, resize, mousemove).
• Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates, requestIdleCallback for low-priority work and a Web Worker for CPU-heavy tasks.
• Split long tasks (over 50 ms) into chunks so input stays responsive (good INP).

expert.content:
Big lists, bundles and the network

• Virtualise long lists: render only visible rows (react-window, TanStack Virtual) instead of thousands of DOM nodes.
• Ship less JavaScript: code-split routes, tree-shake, remove unused dependencies (check with a bundle analyser), lazy-load below-the-fold components and images (loading="lazy").
• Network: HTTP caching headers, compression (Brotli), a CDN, modern image formats (AVIF/WebP) with correct sizes, preconnect/preload for critical resources, and avoid request waterfalls by fetching in parallel.
• Algorithms still matter: replacing an O(n²) nested search with a Map/Set lookup beats micro-optimisations.

interviewQA: Debounce vs throttle?
Debounce delays execution until calls have stopped for a given time (good for search input). Throttle guarantees at most one execution per interval while events keep firing (good for scroll/resize).
What are Core Web Vitals?
Google's user-centred metrics: LCP (loading speed of the main content), INP (responsiveness to interactions) and CLS (visual stability).
What is list virtualisation?
Rendering only the rows visible in the viewport (plus a small buffer) and recycling them as the user scrolls, so very long lists keep a small DOM and stay fast.

cheatNotes: let / const - Block-scoped variable declarations (ES6)
var - Function-scoped, hoisted, legacy declaration
typeof - Returns a string naming a value's type
Template literals - `Hello ${name}` for string interpolation

Closure - A function that retains access to its outer scope's variables
this - Refers to the calling context; varies by how a function is invoked
DOM - In-memory tree representation of an HTML document
addEventListener() - Attaches an event callback without overwriting others
Event bubbling - Events propagate from target up through ancestor elements
Event delegation - One listener on a parent handles events from many children
Array methods - map(), filter(), reduce(), forEach() for functional-style iteration
Destructuring - Unpack array/object values into variables in one line
Spread (...) - Expands an array/object into individual elements/properties
Rest (...) - Collects remaining function arguments into an array

async / await - Syntax for writing Promise-based code sequentially
Promise.all() - Runs Promises concurrently; fulfils when all fulfil but REJECTS on the first rejection. Promise.allSettled() is the one that waits for every promise to settle
JSON.stringify() / JSON.parse() - Convert between JS objects and JSON text
localStorage / sessionStorage - Browser key-value storage APIs
